Specifically, we compare to the state-of-the-art unpaired captioning methods (Honda et al., 2021; Laina et al., 2019) and variants of CLIP based decoding methods: CLIP-Infer that uses CLIP to guide GPT2 at inference, CLIP- Infer-Style which runs CLIP-Infer with our styleaugmented GPT2 generator and CLIP-Retrieval that retrieves caption with the highest CLIP cosine similarity from the training data. According to the standard BLEU-4, Meteor, and CIDEr automatic evaluation metrics, ESPER achieves superior performance against previous state-of-the-art methods and CLIP based decoding algorithms. As stated in previous literature, we also reaffirm that style of the text affects the automatic evaluation to a great deal: ESPER-Free, which does not know COCO caption text style, falls behind ESPER-Style (which has been pretrained on unaligned COCO captions, with the prefix caption:). Finally, note that the computation overhead of ESPER on inference is almost negligible compared to that of CLIP-Infer, a decoding time method. On inference time, ESPER’s runtime is comparable to vanilla GPT-2 alone. Only the lightweight encoder needs to run on top of GPT-2, offering fast inference speed. 3.1.2 Finetuning As our policy network shares the same architecture with MLP-variant CLIPCap, we can directly evaluate the contribution of our encoder as pretrained weights in a supervised setting. In Table 2, we show ESPER initialization bests random initialization both when updating and fixing GPT parameters. Thus, our framework can provide efficient initial alignment between two pretrained modules. 3.2 Evaluation of Auditory Alignment We extend ESPER to another modality: audio. As an auditory counterpart of CLIP, we use Wav2CLIP to score the audiolinguistic alignment during RL training, but otherwise, the setup remains the same. Here, we break the pairing in an audio captioning dataset Audio- Caps to evaluate unpaired audio captioning performance. We follow an identical evaluation protocol as in § 3.1, except that we only use audio as input. In Table 3, we only report the performance of GPT-2-based baselines, as the unpaired image baselines (Laina et al., 2019; Honda et al., 2021) require object detectors and cannot be directly applied. ESPER achieves better results than baseline models, which first rollout random text samples conditioned on fixed (e.g. Sound of a) or the oracle prompts and then select ones with maximal CLIP cosine similarity. Also, the style prompt tuning positively contributes to ESPER ‘s performance, increasing CIDEr by 4.86. Wav2CLIP (and preliminary experiments with other audio encoders, specifically,; which are also pretrained on an audio classifica- tion dataset (Gemmeke et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2020a)) appears to provide less accurate training signal for ESPER compared to image CLIP pretrained on large-scale image caption dataset. We expect this is the case not only because audio classification datasets are relatively small but also because these datasets do not offer rich natural language annotations. Still, our model can generate audio-relevant and plausible captions as described in Figure 8. 3.3 Generalization to Diverse Styles We now experiment beyond standard image captioning setups to demonstrate ESPER’s capacity to generate image-related texts of diverse styles. Here, we evaluate two styles that can be supported by existing public corpora: visual news and dialogue. 3.3.1 Visual News VisualNews includes 1.08 million news images along with associated image captions and articles, sourced from four news sites. The captions describe the image’s relevance to the news article instead of simply describing the literal image contents. For our experiments, we assign respective style prefixes per news source. For a fair comparison, we compare ESPER with models that rely only on image inputs,3 e.g., Show Attend Tell, from. We also include the text-only style generator without visual inputs as another baseline (Text-Only). Results are in Table 4: zero-shot ESPER outperforms not only the text-only baseline but also the supervised baseline in Bleu-4 and METEOR scores. However, it lags behind the supervised model by a wide margin in CIDEr terms of CIDEr. We attribute this difference to a combined effect of the news style and CLIP: while news consists of a myriad of proper nouns, CLIP has not been exposed to a majority of such terms. As a result, ESPER does not generate as many proper nouns as in the ground truth captions, decreasing the CIDEr score, which takes the rarity of terms into account. By finetuning the adaptor, ESPER overcomes this knowledge gap and surpasses the baselines even in the CIDEr score. 3Other baselines for VisualNews generate based on the article text or keywords as inputs and hence are not directly comparable to our framework. ■ CLIP-Infer ■ CLIP-Infer-Style ■ ESPER-Style ■ Human Caption. Given an image and previous dialogue act, the model is asked to rank the likelihood of the 100 answer candidates. After training ESPER with the unpaired dialogue style generator backbone, we rank the answer candidates by likelihood of the answers given the image and the question. We use the validation set for evaluation for fair comparison against previously reported zero-shot baseline results. The baselines consist of ViLBERT and frozen ViLBERT finetuned with a linear head. The bottom half of Table 4 shows the VisDial dataset re-ranking results. Zero-shot ESPER improves the baselines by a margin. It even outperforms the supervised ViLBERT-Head, showing that ESPER is capable of discerning likely visual dialogues. 3.4 From One Image to Many Styles While we observe that ESPER can generate diverse image-related texts, we still need to prove that this diversity in style is induced by text prompts. A null hypothesis is that there are identifiable and consistent features found, e.g., only in news articles. The model may have exploited this superficial relation to generating news style captions. ESP dataset from Section 3 is specifically designed to counter this hypothesis as it exhibits multiple styled texts for the same image. Figure 5 we show that ESPER can generate diverse text depending on textual style prompts. ESPER outperforms CLIPCap-MLP, a COCO-supervised baseline, demonstrating prompt-conditioned generation is necessary to handle ESP dataset. Also, the text-only baseline falls by a wide margin, indicating that the visuallinguistic alignment is as important as the text diversity. Finally, ESPER-Style improves over ESPER- Free to show the effect of explicit style conditioning. Each sample is evaluated by three annotators using the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform. The results are shown in Figure 4. On average, ESPER provides more visually relevant and informative content in every prompt than CLIP-Infer. In most cases, CLIP-Infer generally produces short generations; and, because it wasn’t designed to adapt to individual styles, it cannot as effectively generalize to custom prompts. Figure 8 additionally demonstrates that ESPER can also adapt to the audio via wav2clip rewards. Related Work Visual-Language Pretraining. Successful visionlanguage models pretrained on large-scale imagetext corpora have been proposed, e.g., BERT- style models;;;, encoder-decoder style models,;; and constrastive models (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021a). Vision-text models have additionally been extended to audio (Zhao et al., 2021; Zellers et al., 2022). TAPM adapts visual encoder and GPT with self-supervised training objective that predicts causal order of the visual story. Multimodal prompt tuning. Prefix tuning and Prompt tuning simplify finetuning large models by all but a small number of parameters. adapt prefix tuning to images via maximum likelihood training a small image-to-text adapter using Conceptual Captions. Like ESPER, CLIPCap combines GPT + CLIP image features to generate image caption. We use the same architecture as in CLIPCap and fix GPT weights likewise, effectively following the setup of p-tuning. Unsupervised captioning. To learn visuallinguistic relationship without paired data, previous literature draws upon pseudo-pairing retrieved with visual concept detector or joint image-language embedding space. Most related to our work is that uses CLIP image-text alignment score to guide inference of pretrained language model without further training. Reinforcement learning for language tasks. In image captioning, RL has been used to resolve the discrepancy between training and inference data (Ranzato et al., 2016; Bengio et al., 2015) or to optimize discrete language metrics directly. Storytelling models employ RL to maintain coherence in the story or incorporate human feedback. RL is also proven effective in goal-driven dialogue, interactive QA, grounded generation in text games (Hausknecht et al., 2020; Wang* et al., 2022) and value alignment to human preferences (Nahian et al., 2020; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Ammanabrolu et al., 2022b). Recently, Instruction GPT shows RL can improve prompt-conditioned generation quality of pretrained language models. To the best of our knowledge, ESPER is the first method to use multimodal reward to align images to pretrained language models; while used CLIP rewards as well they finetune an already trained image captioning model instead of a general large language model. Conclusion ESPER combines language generation capability in GPT-2 with multimodal knowledge in CLIP to build a diverse image-conditioned text generator: instead of maximum likelihood training, we train via reinforcement learning rewards. We note that the RL objective we consider can be used in conjunction with multimodal prompt tuning and zero-shot captioning with CLIP guidance. Future work includes: 1. enhancing ESPER so that it can simultaneously maximize rewards for multiple modalities (Image, Audio, OCR, Motion in video, etc.); 2. scaling up the CLIP and GPT-2 backbones to larger variants; and 3. exploring the utility of ESPER as a data augmentation tool for multimodal reasoning tasks.

papers.title: A Unified Framework for Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning
papers.abstract: Zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a setting for developing general agents, capable of solving downstream tasks without additional training or planning at test-time. While conventional RL optimizes policies for fixed rewards, zero-shot RL requires learning representations that enable immediate adaptation to arbitrary reward functions. As the field matures, the growing diversity of approaches demands a foundational framework reconciling different perspectives under a common unifying structure. In this work, we introduce a formal, unified framework for zero-shot RL, allowing for rigorous comparisons across methods. papers.full_text: Zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a setting for developing general agents, capable of solving downstream tasks without additional training or planning at test-time. While conventional RL optimizes policies for fixed rewards, zero-shot RL requires learning representations that enable immediate adaptation to arbitrary reward functions. As the field matures, the growing diversity of approaches demands a foundational framework reconciling different perspectives under a common structure. In this work, we introduce a formal, unified framework for zero-shot RL, allowing for rigorous comparisons across methods. We propose a taxonomy organizing the algorithmic landscape along two levels: representation, distinguishing between compositional and direct methods based on their exploitation of value function decompositions; and learning paradigm, differentiating between reward-free and pseudo reward-free training. Additionally, we propose a unified view of existing error bounds, decomposing the total error into three primary contributing components: inference, reward, and approximation, serving as a foundation for more grounded comparisons of zeroshot methods. Introduction The reinforcement learning (RL; Sutton & Barto 2020) objective is commonly defined as identifying a policy that maximizes the expected cumulative reward. While this paradigm has enabled remarkable progress across diverse domains (Berner et al., 2019; Mirhoseini et al., 2021; Mankowitz et al., 2023; Seo et al., 2024), it is limited by its dependence on a single reward function, hindering the ability to transfer to new objectives. Unsupervised RL relaxes this dependence by enabling agents to acquire environment knowledge in a taskagnostic pre-training phase, allowing for efficient fine-tuning once an extrinsic reward is revealed. Zeroshot RL takes this paradigm to its limit: agents must adapt to downstream tasks immediately after pre-training, requiring representations to be expressive enough for near-optimal behaviors to be extracted directly, without any task-specific fine-tuning, planning, or substantial computation. The zero-shot paradigm has emerged as a candidate for training behavioral foundation models, the RL analogue of foundation models; an area where RL has historically lagged behind, motivating further research in the field. Recently, zero-shot RL has received increasing attention, resulting in a diverse set of proposed algorithms (Hansen et al., 2020; Liu & Abbeel, 2021; Frans et al., 2024; Agarwal et al., 2025b; Cetin et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025), covering a wide range of algorithmic principles and design choices. In this work, we establish the first unified framework for the field, introducing a taxonomy that groups methods according to their shared principles and underlying differences. This taxonomy, together with a consistent notation, provides the structure needed to navigate the zero-shot landscape. Note that our framework focuses on zero-shot-specific algorithmic paradigms and not, for example, on representation learning strategies within a given zero-shot paradigm. Each class in our framework is illustrated with a small set of representative examples from the literature. As such, our intention is to add structure to the field, not to fully survey it. We further introduce a unifying lens under which existing error bounds on zero-shot methods can be understood, decomposing the total error into three primary contributing factors. Preliminaries Formally, the reinforcement learning problem is modeled as a Markov Decision Process (MDP) (Stratonovich, 1960; Puterman, 1994), defined as a tuple M = (S, A, p, p0, r, γ). Here, S is the state space, A is the action space, p0 ∈ ∆(S) is the initial state distribution, p(s′|s, a) ∈ ∆(S) is the transition function, r(s, a, s′) is the bounded reward function (see Appendix B for details of the reduction of arguments) and γ ∈ [0, 1) is the discount factor. The behavior of an agent interacting with this MDP is defined by a policy π ∈ Π, that is, a mapping π: S → ∆(A) assigning a distribution over actions to each state. The value function V π(s) denotes the expected discounted return starting from state s and following policy π, V π(s) = Eπ,p[�∞ t=0 γt r(st, at)|s0 = s], resulting in the RL objective π∗(·|s) = arg maxπ∈Π V π(s). A core concept in unsupervised RL is that of occupancy measures. The successor representation (SR; Dayan 1993) is simplest formulation of this concept. Formally, in a discrete MDP, for a given policy π, the SR is defined as the expected discounted future occupancy of state s+ starting from state s: M π(s, s+) = Eπ,p � �∞ t=0 γt1{st = s+} | s0 = s �. (1) This representation allows for a linear decoupling of the MDP dynamics from the reward function, where the value function is recovered as V π(s) = � s+∈S M π(s, s+)r(s+), providing a theoretical basis for zero-shot evaluation of a policy under varying rewards. Zero-Shot RL In the zero-shot setting, we consider a family of MDPs, MR ≡ {(S, A, p, p0, r, γ) | r ∈ R}, where R denotes a specified set of reward functions under consideration, which may represent the space of all possible rewards or just a subset of tasks or skills of interest. Under this setting, training is decoupled from task-specific feedback: while the agent may observe rewards during training, these signals are arbitrary and non-informative of the downstream tasks. At inference, reward functions are drawn from a distribution of downstream tasks Dtest, which is unknown during training. The objective is to obtain optimal policies π∗ r for all r ∈ Dtest without additional parameter optimization (fine-tuning), explicit planning (i.e. reasoning over state transitions to synthesize new behaviors), or substantial computation. Fine-tuning and planning are prohibited as both produce policies not already encoded in the learned representation: finetuning by drawing on additional test-time data, planning by synthesizing new behaviors through an auxiliary structure such as a world model, contradicting the premise of zero-shot adaptation. The third constraint, computation itself, is formalized in Section 3.3 through the notion of instant extraction. The objective for zero-shot RL can formally be expressed as π∗ = arg max π∈Π Er∼Dtest[Ep0,πr(·|s),p[ �∞ t=0 γt r(st, at, st+1)]]. (2) Framework Our taxonomy categorizes the space of zero-shot methods by identifying two primary decision nodes: representation and learning paradigm. At the first level, we distinguish between methods based on their representation, partitioned into direct and compositional approaches. The taxonomy further divides based on the learning paradigm: reward-free vs. pseudo reward-free. This hierarchical decomposition, illustrated in Figure 1, serves as the basis for our framework. The following section provides a breakdown and formal definitions of these design primitives. 3.1 Representation: Direct vs. Compositional Direct methods provide a conceptually straightforward approach to zero-shot RL by learning a rewardconditioned value function Qr(s, a), also known as a universal value function. In contrast, compositional methods decompose the value function by learning an intermediate target, enabling the reconstruction of task-specific value functions during inference. Direct representations learn a direct mapping from state-action and reward to optimal values: Q∗: S × A × R → R, (s, a, r) �→ Q∗ r(s, a). (3) Q∗ r = F(µ, r) F = Idµ µr(s, a) HILP (4.2) FRE (4.3) pseudo − direct F ̸= Idµ µr(s, a) USF (5.2) FB (5.4) pseudo µπ(s, a) SF&GPI (5.1) PSM (5.5) compositional Representation Learning Paradigm Figure 1: Taxonomy of zero-shot RL methods, organized along two axes that jointly determine how each method recovers the optimal action-value function Q∗ r = F(µ, r) from a learned representation µ and a reward function r. The first split (representation) separates direct methods from compositional methods: direct methods define µ as the value function itself µ = Q∗ r, so the decomposition operator reduces to the identity, F = Idµ; compositional methods instead define µ as some intermediate representation that requires a non-trivial operator, F ̸= Idµ, to reconstruct task-specific value functions. The second split (learning paradigm) separates pseudo reward-free training (dashed boxes), where the target µr(s, a) is conditioned on the reward function, from reward-free training (solid boxes), where the target µπ(s, a) is learned independently of any reward. Because direct representations are reward-conditioned by construction, a reward-free direct method is structurally infeasible, marked by the grayed-out node (−). Under this direct mapping, the function approximator must capture the complete reward-induced structure, yielding Q∗ values directly from (s, a, r), with no explicit substructure between policy, occupancy, and value. Policy extraction for a target task r ∼ Dtest is performed via π∗ r(s) ∈ arg maxa Q∗(s, a, r). Compositional representations explicitly leverage the structure of the value function. Under this approach, the learning problem reduces to estimating individual components, that are recombined at inference time according to the specified substructure. More formally, compositional methods learn representations µ(s, a), which allow to infer optimal values via some structure in the form of a decomposition operator F: Q∗ r(s, a) = F(µ, r), (4) where the operator F encodes the relationship between the learned representation and the reward. An instantiation of F could be as simple as the inner product between some reward representation f(r) and the target, i.e. F(µ, r) = ⟨µ, f(r)⟩, as for the successor representation (cf. Eq. 1). Notably, as shown in Figure 1, direct representations constitute the special case where µr = Q∗ r, or equivalently F = Idµ. Because we define compositional methods to be everything that is not direct, we assume compositional methods to have a non-trivial decomposition operator F ̸= Idµ. 3.2 Learning Paradigm: Reward-free vs. Pseudo reward-free At test time, the agent is evaluated under an unknown reward distribution Dtest, to which it has no access during training. Consequently, it must either adopt a reward-free training paradigm or define an arbitrary set of reward functions to guide the learning process (pseudo reward-free). Reward-free methods learn a policy-conditioned quantity µπ(s, a) – always superscribed by π – through objectives that are entirely independent of reward signals. By definition, this paradigm excludes any objective relying on reward maximization (i.e. Bellman optimality backups). Therefore, as illustrated in Figure 1, reward-free objectives only exist in the context of compositional representations. As an example, consider a discrete-space MDP and the successor representation of a fixed policy π, denoted as M π, learned by minimizing the TD-error of the SR following π. The representation is compositional because it targets a component of the value function; as such, we denote it as µπ = M π, with superscript π because it is learned via a reward-free objective. Assuming that the policy space Π is large enough, that is, containing the optimal policy for all r ∈ R Zero-shot adaptation to any reward r ∈ R, is performed via the operator F as Q∗ r = F(µπ, r) = maxπ∈Π⟨M π, r⟩. Pseudo reward-free methods, in contrast, leverage reward signals to learn representations contingent on a reward function, denoted by µr(s, a). The agent is provided access to a training distribution of random rewards, r ∼ Dtrain, which are non-informative of the downstream tasks, resulting in a form of self-supervised RL. The underlying principle is that by sampling a sufficiently diverse set of random reward functions during training, the resulting representation space will cover the rewards encountered during inference. Finally, we formalize the preceding concepts into a unified zero-shot RL framework. Unified Zero-Shot RL Framework Training Define µ(s, a) and a compatible learning paradigm such that Q∗ r = F(µ, r) ∀r ∈ R (5) Policy Extraction Given a (unseen) reward r ∼ Dtest extract a policy via π∗ r(·|s) = arg max a F(µ, r) (6) 3.3 The Zero-shot Boundary Our framework exposes an ambiguity in the definition of zero-shot RL: how much computation is the decomposition operator F allowed at test time? Fine-tuning µ and explicit planning are clearly ruled out, but beyond the vague prohibition on “substantial computation” no upper bound on the cost of F has been specified. We propose the notion of instant extraction as a reference point. An operator F admits instant extraction if its cost is O(1) in |Π|, that is, if extraction does not scale with the number of behaviors encoded in µ. Pseudo reward-free methods satisfy this: the policy is obtained by a single conditioning operation on the desired reward, independently of what µ encodes. This is zero-shot RL in the strictest sense. However, not every method commonly accepted as zero-shot meets this criterion. A test-time search over the policies already encoded in µ has cost growing with |Π| and so fails instant extraction, yet it only selects among represented behaviors rather than synthesizing new ones, and completes in a modest number of operations under mild assumptions. It is unclear at what point such a search ceases to be zero-shot. Fixing a universal bound on F is impractical given the diversity of extraction procedures. We therefore propose to treat instant extraction as the strict end of the zero-shot definition and to position each method’s F relative to it. Methods that admit instant extraction are unambiguously zero-shot; beyond that lies a fuzzy region, and a method’s distance from instant extraction gives an axis along which to place it. In the following sections we review key zero-shot methods starting with direct methods in Section 4, and moving to compositional in Section 5. In Section 6, we analyze error bounds for different algorithms under a common lens, categorizing the total error into three primary components showing how design choices affect the error. An extensive list of zero-shot methods categorized under our taxonomy can be found in Table A. Direct Representations Methods relying on direct representations (left branch in Figure 1) parameterize and optimize the value function directly. The training objective is the optimal value function itself, µr(s, a) = Q∗ r(s, a). While some methods instead learn a parameterized policy π∗ r(s) ∈ ∆(A), this often serves as a practical workaround for the intractability of arg maxa Q∗ r(s, a) (Lillicrap et al., 2016; Fujimoto et al., 2018). Because we are only concerned with optimal behavior for each task, direct representations implicitly parameterize each policy by the reward function for which it is optimal. This approach is usually facilitated via an embedding function f: R → Z that maps reward functions into a latent representation space. This allows us to index the set of optimal policies by Z, where πz represents the optimal policy for the reward function embedded as z = f(r). Defining a task space While f could theoretically be the identity mapping, this becomes intractable in continuous or high-dimensional settings. Consequently, training direct representations generally involves two phases: (i) define or learn a task encoder f: R �→ Z; (ii) train some representation of optimal action-value functions or policies µf(r) using rewards r sampled from some distribution until convergence. Since the second phase corresponds to standard RL training for each sampled reward, the primary challenge lies in the first phase: learning an encoder f that defines a task space Z expressive enough to retain all rewardrelevant information while remaining sufficiently smooth to enable generalization through µ. Since the space of admissible rewards is vast, the effectiveness of generalization critically depends on how the chosen prior constrains and shapes coverage of plausible downstream tasks. In addition, task embeddings suffer from inherent identifiability issues: distinct reward functions may yield indistinguishable behaviors, making the corresponding task representations fundamentally ambiguous. In the following, we present three methods that successfully define or learn such a space. 4.1 Goal-Conditioned RL A canonical example of such an embedding arises in goal-conditioned RL (GCRL; Schaul et al. 2015; Andrychowicz et al. 2017; Levy et al. 2019; Chebotar et al. 2021; Eysenbach et al. 2022; Park et al. 2023), where tasks are limited to goal reaching. In this setting, the reward embedding emerges naturally: each task is defined by a goal state, giving rise to the natural identification Z = S. 4.2 Hilbert Representations The Hilbert Representations framework (HILP; Park et al. 2024) defines a geometric abstraction of the state space by learning a mapping ϕ: S → Z, where Z is a Hilbert space, such that distances in the latent space correspond to temporal distances in the original MDP. Using this, we can define a goal-reaching reward function for any vector in latent space via rz(s, s′):= (ϕ(s′) − ϕ(s))⊤z, rewarding transitions that align with the direction of the goal z. Through rz(s, s′), optimal policies π∗ z can be trained for all z ∈ Z. At test time, given a reward function r, the optimal behavior for any task can be recovered by πf(r) for f(r) = arg minz∈Z[(r(s, a, s′) − rz(s, s′))2]. 4.3 Functional Reward Encoding Restricting the task space to goal-reaching is not intrinsic to direct representations. The Functional Reward Encoding framework (FRE; Frans et al., 2024) introduces a method to embed arbitrary reward functions into a latent space fe: R → Z. A state-dependent reward function r: S → R is represented by a set of samples {(si, r(si))}i∈I, which a permutation-invariant transformer encodes into a latent vector z ∈ Z. To ensure z captures generalizable features of the reward landscape, an encoder-decoder architecture is trained using an information-bottleneck objective over a reward distribution Dtrain comprised of goal-reaching, linear, and random MLP functions. Then, networks Q(·, z), V (·, z), and π(·, z) are trained using Implicit Q- Learning under sampled reward functions projected into the latent space Z via the frozen encoder. Relation to Framework For all direct methods, the training target is the optimal action-value function itself, i.e. µ = Q∗ r. In general, µ cannot be conditioned directly on the reward function, as the reward space is generally intractable; instead, a suitable reward representation f: R → Z is required such that µf(r) = Q∗ r. Given a reward function r, a policy can then be extracted as πr(·|s) = arg maxa µf(r)(s, a). Compositional Representations Compositional methods (right branch in Figure 1) are built on occupancy measures such as the SR (Eq. 1). They aim to capture the occupancy measure of a set of policies, including the degenerate case of a single policy, and to extract relevant behavior given a reward, either through an explicit search at test time or by shifting this cost to pretraining via inductive biases. Such methods can be rewardfree (Sections 5.1, 5.5) or pseudo reward-free (Sections 5.2, 5.4). This section covers the key zero-shot methods together with their foundational objects (Sections 5.1, 5.3), organized by conceptual evolution rather than training paradigm: starting from basic approaches, we trace how subsequent methods address specific limitations or pursue distinct directions. 5.1 Successor Features Successor Features (SF; Barreto et al. 2017) extend the SR to continuous MDPs by tracking expected discounted future features instead of states. Assume a feature mapping ϕ: S × A × S → Rd for some d ∈ N, and suppose that the reward function can be linearly decomposed as r(s, a, s′) = ϕ(s, a, s′)⊤w, (7) where w ∈ Rd is a weight vector and ϕ(s, a, s′) ∈ Rd are the basic features of the one-step transition (s, a, s′). Note, that for a single reward function, such a decomposition always exists (e.g., ϕ(s, a, s′) = r(s, a, s′) and w = 1). Following Eq. 1, the successor features of a policy π are defined as ψπ(s, a):= Eπ,p ��∞ t=0 γtϕ(st, at, st+1) ��� s0 = s, a0 = a �. (8) Just as the SR decouples dynamics from rewards, SFs decouple dynamics from the reward weights w. Given a reward embedding w and basic features ϕ, the action-value function under policy π can be recovered as Qπ r (s, a) = ψπ(s, a)⊤w. This decomposition allows for zero-shot policy evaluation: the performance of π can be evaluated on any task in the span of ϕ by simply updating w. Training Analogous to value functions, successor features satisfy a Bellman-like recursion: ψπ(s, a) = Es′∼p, a′∼π[ϕ(s, a, s′) + γψπ(s′, a′)]. (9) Allowing ψπ to be learned using standard temporal-difference (TD) methods. While the linearity assumption of Eq. 7 may appear restrictive, the framework can still be applied when ϕ only approximately linearizes rewards by considering the best linear approximation ˜wr such that r ≈ ϕ⊤ ˜wr. For instance, ˜wr can be obtained by minimizing the mean squared error: ˜wr = arg min w E(s,a,s′)∼D �(r(s, a, s′) − ϕ(s, a, s′)⊤w)2�. (10) Generalized Policy Improvement Standard policy improvement identifies a better policy relative to the value function of a single policy, Generalized Policy Improvement (GPI; Barreto et al. 2017) extends this logic to a set of policies {πi}n i=1. Given the respective action-value functions {Qπi}n i=1 under the same reward, we define the GPI policy as the point-wise maximum over the set πGPI(·|s) ∈ arg max a max i Qπi(s, a). (11) Similarly to the standard policy improvement theorem, it can be shown the new policy guarantees that QπGPI(s, a) ≥ maxi Qπi(s, a) for all s ∈ S and a ∈ A. Relation to Framework Pairing SFs with GPI is an instance of a reward-free approach, as the training target µπ = ψπ can be trained without any reward signal. From said target, the optimal value function can be recovered using the decomposition operator F(µπ, r) = maxπ(µπ)w r. In the policy extraction phase, given a reward function r ∼ Dtest, we first calculate ˜wr (Eq. 10), for which we can infer an approximation for the optimal policy via GPI πr(·|s) = arg max a max i ψπi(s, a)⊤ ˜wr. (12) 5.2 Universal Successor Features The scalability of SF&GPI is primarily constrained by the limited generalization across policy space. One might mitigate this issue by conditioning the successor features on the policy itself (i.e. learning ψπ(s, a) as a function of π), yet a naive search over Π at test time remains computationally intensive without significant constraints. Universal Successor Features (USF; Borsa et al., 2019) circumvent this limitation by exploiting the relationship between optimal policies and their inducing reward functions. By parameterizing policies by the reward weights for which they are optimal, we avoid an explicit search over policies during the policy extraction phase. Specifically, for a reward function of the form r = ϕ⊤w, we define πw:= π∗ ϕ⊤w as the optimal policy given the reward weights w. Then, the universal successor features for a family of policies (πw)w∈W are defined as πw(·|s) = arg max a ψ(s, a, w)⊤w, ψ(s, a, w) = ψπw(s, a). (13) Notably, ψ(s, a, w) encodes the successor features for the optimal policy with respect to all rewards admitting the factorization r = ϕ⊤w. Therefore, the policy extraction phase for USF reduces to computing the task vector w as in Eq. 10. Training As with successor features, USF also satisfy a Bellman-like equation, motivating minimization of the Bellman residual to train USFs. Following Eq. 9, we get: L(ψ) = Ew∼pW �δw(t)⊤ δw(t)�, δw(t) = ϕ(st, at, st+1) + γ ψ(st+1, πw(st+1), w) − ψ(st, at, w), (14) where δt w is the temporal-difference error. These objectives are particularly useful when evaluating policies on tasks different from those that induced them, as in GPI. The curse of ϕ Successor Features rely on the assumption that all downstream tasks of interest lie in the linear span of the basic features ϕ (Eq. 7). Unless a unifying object encompassing both ψ and ϕ is introduced, they cannot be learned jointly. In such case, two distinct objectives must be defined: one for ψ and one for ϕ. Choosing an appropriate training objective for learning ϕ is critical, as it determines which aspects of the environment are preserved and, consequently, which reward functions admit accurate linear parameterizations1. Moreover, since ϕ’s objective is defined independently of ψ, nothing guarantees that the resulting features are well-suited for accurately estimating successor features on top of them, potentially compounding error across the two stages. TD-JEPA narrows this gap by training the basic features ϕ and a predictor Tϕ jointly via a single temporal-difference objective: for a family of policies πw(·|s) = arg maxa T ϕ(ϕ(s), a, w)⊤w, defined as for USF above, L(ϕ, T ϕ) = Ew∼pW,a′∼πw(·|s′)[ ��T ϕ(ϕ(s), a, w) − ¯ϕ(s′) − γ ¯T ϕ(¯ϕ(s′), a′, w) ��2], (15) where ¯T ϕ and ¯ϕ indicate target networks. Since this target mirrors the Bellman recursion satisfied by successor features (cf. Eq. 9), Tϕ is trained to approximate the successor features ψ(ϕ(s), a, w) of ϕ. Crucially, ϕ appears in both the prediction and target of the loss, so it is learned jointly with Tϕ. Relation to Framework The training target for USF-based methods is µr = ψ(s, a, wr), allowing to recover the optimal values via the decomposition operator F(µr, r) = (µr)⊤wr. As such, we require some reward representations during training (cf. Eq. 14), rendering this a pseudo reward-free approach. At inference time, given a reward r, we compute ˜wr as Eq. 10 and infer a policy as πr(·|s) = arg maxa ψ(s, a, ˜wr)⊤ ˜wr. 5.3 Successor Measure While feature-based methods adapt successor representations to continuous domains by tracking state properties, the successor measure (SM; Blier et al. 2021) provides a more fundamental generalization. By transitioning from discrete counts to a measure-theoretic framework, it extends the SR to continuous state-action spaces while preserving its core interpretation. We overload the notation by identifying the SM as M, just as with the SR, as the SM naturally encompasses the SR. Formally, the successor measure for a policy π, a state–action pair (s, a) ∈ S ×A, and a set X ⊂ S is defined as M π(s, a, X):= Eπ,p[ �∞ t=0 γt 1{(st, at) ∈ X} | s0 = s, a0 = a]. (16) 1For a comprehensive review of existing feature-learning methods for USF, we refer the reader to. Treating M π as a measure allows us to handle discrete and continuous spaces in a unified way. Let ρ ∈ ∆(S) be a state distribution satisfying ρ(s) > 0 for all s ∈ S, and define the Radon–Nikodym derivative mπ:= dM π dρ, or in other words the density of Mπ with respect to ρ. For γ < 1, Mπ is a finite measure since M π(s, a, S) = (1 − γ)−1, which, together with the assumption on ρ, guarantees that this density exists. We can then express the action–value function under a reward r: S → R as Qπ(s, a) = Es+∼ρ[mπ(s, a, s+) r(s+)]. Training Successor measures follow a Bellman-like relationship, allowing mθ ≈ mπ to be trained via temporal-difference learning, i.e.: L(θ) = Es,a∼ρ,s+∼ρ[(mθ(s, a, s+) − ˆm¯θ(s, a, s+))2], (17) Where the target ˆm¯θ(s, a, s+) = δs(ds+) ρ(ds+) + γEs′+∼p(·|s,a),a′∼π(s′)[m¯θ(s′, a′, s+)]. As in classical RL, the gra- dient of the loss is not propagated through the target, and ¯θ refers to a stop-gradient or target network. Notably, in the following subsections we only have to deal with the Radon-Nikodym density mπ, and assume that ρ is a fixed (data) distribution. Relation to Framework While the SM is not a standalone framework in itself, in its most basic formulation it can describe a reward-free, compositional method with target µπ = mπ, and the optimal value function can be recovered via the decomposition operator F(µπ, r) = max π∈Π Es+∼ρ[µπ(s, a, s+) r(s+)], (18) policy extraction is facilitated as πr(s) = arg maxa maxπ∈Π Es+∼ρ[µπ(s, a, s+) r(s+)]. Notably, if Π is sufficiently expressive, specifically if it contains the optimal policy π∗ for a given reward r, then full state-action coverage (support) is a sufficient condition for recovery of the optimum. In contrast, if the search space is restricted to a single SM, encoding, for example, a behavior policy mπb, coverage alone does not guarantee optimality. Assuming mπb encodes the necessary transitions to define π∗ r, the policy extraction operation arg maxa Es+∼ρ[mπb(s, a, s+)r(s+)] lacks the ability to break the temporal structure induced by the behavior policy itself, making optimality guarantees a function of both temporal structure and coverage. Nonetheless, an approach following this framework, has shown good empirical performance. Lastly, it should be noted that SF and SM are related as ψπ(s, a) = Es+∼ρ[mπ(s, a, s+)ϕ(s+)]. 5.4 Forward-Backward Representation Approaches that directly approximate the successor measure have the advantage of tracking successor states rather than features, thus not requiring a secondary objective to learn the basic features. Forward-Backward representations (FB; Blier et al., 2021; Touati & Ollivier, 2021; Touati et al., 2023) factorize the successor measure into a low-rank decomposition: mπ(s, a, s+) = F(s, a)⊤B(s+), (19) where F: S × A → Rd and B: S → Rd. As for the SM, reward-free objectives can be defined for FB, such as Eq. (17). However, naive policy-conditioned approaches may suffer from an expensive test-time search over the representation to extract the optimal policy. Later works, propose to employ a similar strategy to that of USF to FB, namely, relating policy parametrization and rewards. For a parametric family of policies (πz)z∈Z, we define the forward backward representation as as a pair of functions F: S × A × Z → Z and B: S → Z such that for all z ∈ Z, (s, a) ∈ S × A πz(·|s) = arg max a F(s, a, z)⊤z, mπz(s, a, s+) = F(s, a, z)⊤B(s+). (20) Crucially, for any bounded reward function r, by defining z as the reward projection zr:= Es∼ρ[B(s)r(s)] we can recover the optimal value function as Q∗ r(s, a) = F(s, a, zr)⊤zr (Theorem 2 of Touati & Ollivier, 2021). Analogously to USF, FB aligns the policy and reward spaces by conditioning a family of optimal policies on a task-specific latent z. However, FB departs from USF in its theoretical expressivity: whereas USF is constrained by a pre-defined set of basic features ϕ, FB can in theory represent any reward function. Training Training is performed by minimizing a loss similar to that of Eq. (17) where we additionally sample over the space of reward embeddings Z. L(F, B) = Es,a∼ρ,s+∼ρ,z∼pZ[(mFz,B(s, a, s+) − ˆm ¯ Fz, ¯ B(s, a, s+))2], (21) where mFz,B is a parametric version of mπz. With δρ(s+) = δs(ds+) ρ(ds+), the target is calculated as ˆm ¯ Fz, ¯ B(s, a, s+) = δρ(s+) + γEs′∼p(·|s,a),a′∼πz(·|s′)[ ˆm ¯ Fz, ¯ B(s′, a′, s+)]. In continuous spaces, the hard maximum over actions is replaced by either a softmax or a z-conditioned policy network. To resolve the scale ambiguity in the factorization F ⊤B an auxiliary orthonormalization loss enforcing Eρ[BB⊤] ≈ I is added. Relation to Framework In FB representations, the training target is the joint representation µr = (F, B). Due to the intrinsic coupling between policy and reward, training an FB representation constitutes a pseudo reward-free approach: although it aims to generalize across rewards, it still requires access to task embeddings during training in order to optimize its objective. For a given reward function r, its corresponding representation can be obtained as zr(B) = Es∼ρ[r(s)B(s)], which induces the following decomposition: F(µ = (F, B), r) = F(s, a, zr(B))⊤zr(B). (22) Policy inference is then performed accordingly via πr(·|s) = arg maxa F(s, a, zr(B))⊤zr(B). 5.5 Proto Successor Measure Proto Successor Measure (PSM; Agarwal et al., 2025b) takes a reward-free approach to learning the space of successor measures. Extracting the optimal policy from such representation requires a search. PSM exploits properties of the SM to define a tractable search over such space. The SM admits a linear decomposition mπy(s, a, s+) = Φ(s, a, s+)⊤y + b(s, a, s+), where the basis function Φ: S × A × S → Rd and bias term b: S × A × S → R are policy-independent. The policy πy is represented by the weight vector y ∈ Rd. This linear decomposition allows to cast the zero-shot objective under the dual linear programming formulation (LP). Specifically, the objective is to find a y, that maximizes some reward function r. We can ensure the search is constrained to only valid successor measures by applying a non-negativity constraint, resulting in the following objective for extracting the optimal policy weights y∗: y∗ = arg max y Es∼p0,a∼πy(·|s),s+∼ρ[mπy(s, a, s+)r(s+)] s.t. mπy(s, a, s+) ≥ 0 ∀ (s, a, s+), (23) The expectations over p0 and πy are intractable since we lack access to these distributions, and are replaced by expectations over transitions from the dataset ρ, restricting coverage to the support of the behavior policy. The non-negativity constraint is rendered tractable by relaxing it into a soft Lagrangian penalty. Training In discrete MDPs, the components of the representation can be learned by minimizing an objective similar to Eq. 17. To allow sampling over policies, we define a discrete family of policies (πv)v∈V, with V ⊆ Z; an additional parametric function y: Z → Rd maps each policy identifier onto a vector. The components are individually parametrized and learned by minimizing a reward-free objective over the dataset of transitions and policies, resulting in the following loss L(Φ, y, b) = Es,a∼ρ, s+∼ρ,v∼pV[(mΦ,y(v),b(s, a, s+) − ˆm¯Φ,¯y(v),¯b(s, a, s+))2], (24) where mΦ,y(v),b is a parametric version of mπy(v). The target is calculated similarly to FB, Eq. 21. Given a learned representation, the policy extraction phase requires solving the LP in Eq. 23, from which we obtain the SM of the optimal policy. Relation to Framework The representation in PSM does not exploit ties between rewards and policies, making this a reward-free, compositional method. This also allows the representation to be learned through Bellman evaluation backups, avoiding the possible instabilities caused by the maximization over the actionvalue function, typical of optimality backups. This methods exhibit the same decomposition operator as the SM, defined by Eq. 18. Based on this decomposition operator, policy extraction is performed via the search defined in Eq. 23, resulting in the optimal parameters y∗ that define the extracted policy. Error Decompositions All previously introduced methods are theoretically well-founded and recover the optimal value function in the idealized setting via Q∗ r = F(µ, r). While optimality is theoretically attainable, practical implementations, constrained by factors such as finite model capacity, restricted search spaces, and approximate expectations, incur three primary sources of error: • Inference Error: In some cases it might not be possible to exactly evaluate the decomposition operator. For instance, when F requires a search over the full policy space, such as in SF&GPI. • Reward Error: Even with access to the true reward function, reward embedding-based methods may suffer from errors introduced by the latent representation itself. • Approximation Error: We always recover an approximate variant of the true µ, due to limited data and computational resources. In this section we build on existing results to establish error bounds for the individual zero-shot methods introduced above under a common error decomposition. Informally, given our extracted policy ˜π = arg maxa ˜F(˜µ, ˜r) we establish error bounds of the generic form ∥Q∗ r − Q˜π r ∥ ≤ C1 ∥ ˜F − F∥ � �� � + C2 ∥˜r − r∥ � �� � εreward + C3 ∥˜µ − µ∥ � �� � εapprox. (25) These bounds enable a qualitative comparison of the methods presented in this work and expose the structural assumptions under which individual error terms vanish by construction. We complement this with a smallscale empirical study (cf. Figure 2), which confirms that this behavior is observable in practice, but also that there is no free lunch: methods incur comparable total error and merely trade off its sources. For readability, the main text states reduced versions of the theorems; full statements, proofs, exact constants, and norm definitions are deferred to Appendix C. Successor Features & GPI We extend the results of (Barreto et al., 2017; Borsa et al., 2019) to account for approximate reward linearizations: Theorem 6.1. Let ϕ be a bounded basic feature mapping, let (W, ·⊤·) be an inner product space, let {wi}n i=1 ∈ W be linear weights and let {πi}n i=1 be a set of the corresponding policies, such that πi is optimal on ϕ⊤wi. Let ˜ψi(s, a) denote the learned SF for the given policies. Let r ∈ R be a bounded reward function and wr its approximate linearization such that r ≈ ϕ⊤wr, and let π(·|s) = arg maxa maxi∈[n] ˜ψi(s, a)⊤wr be the GPI policy. (26) The first term reflects a restricted policy search: unless an optimal policy for the target reward is contained in the training set, an error during policy extraction is unavoidable. This error can be expected to decrease as the number of trained policies grows. The second term captures reward linearization error, which vanishes only if rewards are exactly linear in ϕ. The final term corresponds to approximation error in learning successor features, as a result from finite model capacity and limited training data. Universal Successor Features In contrast to SF&GPI, USFs remove explicit inference error by parameterizing policies through reward weights. However, generalization across W may increase approximation error, especially in regions where coverage is limited. As a consequence of Theorem 6.1 (using the argument in Borsa et al., 2019) we obtain the following error bound for USFs: Theorem 6.2. Let ϕ be a bounded basic feature mapping, let (W, ·⊤·) be an inner product space, let ˜ψ(·, w) denote the learned USFs for some w ∈ W. Let r ∈ R be a bounded reward function and wr ∈ W its approximate linearization such that r ≈ ϕ⊤wr, and let π(·|s) = arg maxa ˜ψ(s, a, wr)⊤wr be the extracted policy. Let ψwr(·) denote the SFs for the policy optimal on ϕ⊤wr. Then: ∥Q∗ r − Qπ r ∥∞ ≤ Cγ ∥r − ϕ⊤wr∥ + Cr ∥ψwr(·) − ˜ψ(·, wr)∥. (27) Forward-Backward Representation A key distinction of FB representations is that they parametrize the successor measure without imposing any assumption on the reward function, which is reflected in their error bound. Extending the results of by an approximation error term, we obtain: 10−4 10−3 10−2 10−1 SF & GPI 10−4 10−3 10−2 10−1 USF εreward εapprox 10−4 10−3 10−2 10−1 FB Figure 2: Error terms of Eq. 25 versus representation dimension d in Four Rooms (log scale; median and IQR over seeds). Terms absent by construction are omitted. Details in Appendix D. Theorem 6.3. Let ΠM denote the set of all memory-less policies on our family of MDPS MR. For any π ∈ ΠM let mπ denote the successor measure. Let Z be an inner product space and let F, B a forwardbackward representation, that is a pair of functions F: S × A × Z → Z and B: S → Z, with factorization defect επ,z(s, a, s+) = mπ(s, a, s+) − F(s, a, z)⊤B(s+). Let ˜F, ˜B denote their learned versions. Let r ∈ R be a bounded reward function, let ρ ∈ ∆(S) a distribution of states, let zr = Es∼ρ[B(s)r(s)] and let π(·|s) = arg maxa ˜F(s, a, zr)⊤zr, then there exists positive constants Cr,γ, ˜Cr,γ only dependent on r and γ such that ∥Q∗ r − Qπ r ∥∞ ≤ Cr,γ �∥επzr,zr∥ + ∥επ,zr∥� + ˜Cr,γ �∥F(·, zr) − ˜F(·, zr)∥ + ∥F ⊤B − ˜F ⊤ ˜B∥�. (28) The theorem leaves the reference point F, B unspecified. We regard it as the ground truth, i.e. the factorization with minimal (ideally vanishing) defect. Under this reading, the first term in Eq. 28 captures the inference error induced by the factorization defect, that is, the error incurred by not representing the successor measure exactly under the given parametrization. While this inference error is conceptually distinct from the linearization error in USFs, the two are closely related (see Touati & Ollivier, 2021, for a detailed discussion). Unlike USFs, FB does not impose a linear decomposition of the reward function apriori, and therefore incurs no explicit reward approximation error of the form appearing in Eqs. 26 and 27. We conjecture that PSM admits a similarly-composed error bound to FB, where the inference would also be tied to the soft LP. Example 6.4. To illustrate these bounds in practice, we instantiate the decomposition of Eq. 25 in a deterministic Four Rooms grid-world (|S| = 104, |A| = 4, γ = 0.95), small enough that every quantity in Theorems 6.1–6.3 is computed rather than estimated, so that each reported error is attributable to the representation alone. SF-based methods use one-hot block indicators as features ϕ; USF and FB additionally require a model of how ψ varies with the task, for which we use a bilinear model with one RBF per training task; see Appendix D for details. Figure 2 shows the resulting error curves over increasing representation dimension d. There is indeed no free lunch: methods trade error between sources while total error remains of comparable magnitude. USF and SF&GPI incur the same reward error, both assuming a linear reward representation; since ϕ is a block indicator, larger d yields finer blocks and eventually enough capacity to represent every reward function linearly, so this error vanishes. FB incurs no reward error at all. The approximation error is markedly larger for USF and FB than for SF&GPI, which fits a separate object per policy rather than generalizing across the representation space, and it grows with d for the latter two. Finally, the inference error dominates for FB and, at larger d, for SF&GPI, whereas USF incurs none by construction. For FB it decreases with d, as added capacity reduces the factorization defect; for SF&GPI with a fixed number of policies n, it increases with d, since the same policy set covers an increasingly large representation space. These terms also localize where a distribution shift in the reward functions takes effect. For USF and FB it enters through the approximation error: both generalize across tasks, so their fit degrades on rewards far from those seen during training. SF&GPI is trained reward-free and is therefore not affected directly; the shift is instead captured in the inference error, as a mismatch between the rewards whose optimal policies are contained in the baseline set and those encountered at test time. Direct Methods Direct approaches do not rely on value-function decomposition and therefore incur no decomposition-induced inference error: Theorem 6.5. Let Z ⊂ Rd and let f: R → Z ⊂ Rd be a reward embedding. For z ∈ Z let ˜Qz denote some trained direct representation. Let r ∈ R be a bounded reward function and f(r) = zr its reward embedding. Then the value error of direct methods decomposes into ∥Q∗ r − ˜Qf(r)∥∞ ≤ inf ˜r∈f −1({zr}) Å 1 − γ ∥r − ˜r∥ + ∥Q∗ ˜r − ˜Qzr∥ ã. (29) In general, the pre-image of a reward embedding contains more than one element: compressing the reward space into a latent space Z forces distinct reward functions onto the same embedding. A single ˜Qz can then not accurately approximate all Q∗ r with r ∈ f −1({z}) simultaneously, and the severity of this effect is affected by how much these optimal value functions differ across the pre-image. Non-identifiability thus comes at a price: even if every reward function is representable in the latent space (which is not guaranteed, so a reward error may already be incurred) and the reward error can be driven to zero, the approximation error is expected to grow with the degree of compression of f. Related Work Most closely related to our work is the unified framework of, which establishes a formal equivalence of several unsupervised RL objectives via the SM. We instead structure the landscape of zero-shot methods by analyzing the implications of various design choices, offering a complementary view. Unsupervised RL methods (Jaderberg et al., 2017; Eysenbach et al., 2019; Laskin et al., 2021) undergo a pretraining phase (either in an reward-free or pseudo reward-free paradigm) followed by a finetuning phase to an extrinsic reward. Zero-shot RL is a subset of URL, where the finetuning phase is ignored and the agent is evaluated immediately after the pretraining phase. Transfer learning in RL (TL), as surveyed in, improves sample efficiency and generalization across tasks by reusing knowledge from prior experience. TL encompasses paradigms that adapt to changes in all parts of the MDP. Within this broader framework, zero-shot RL can be viewed as a form of transfer where adaptation is restricted to changes in the reward. Model-based RL, as surveyed in, leverages transition dynamics models to plan by unrolling simulated trajectories. While decoupling dynamics from rewards enables flexibility, determining optimal values requires tracing potential futures. Model-based agents therefore adapt to new rewards through test-time search, while zero-shot RL demands fast generalization to novel objectives without explicit test-time planning. Discussion & Conclusion We introduced a unified framework for zero-shot RL, providing structure to a previously fragmented field. Our taxonomy distinguishes methods by representation structure, direct versus compositional, and by learning paradigm, separating reward-free from pseudo reward-free objectives. A unified error decomposition further separates inference, reward, and representation approximation error. This work also highlights several directions for future research. First, direct methods may benefit from advances in representation learning, where smoother reward embeddings could improve generalization (Bengio et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2018). In continuous spaces, greedy policy extraction may introduce out-of-distribution errors, which regularization may mitigate (Jeen et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2025). Reward-free compositional methods instead rely on Bellman evaluation backups, offering a possible way to avoid such compounding errors. While most recent works focus on offline RL to isolate the representation learning problem, the online regime introduces exploration challenges; leveraging zero-shot representations for exploration remains a promising direction (Sun et al., 2025; Urpí et al., 2025). Finally, existing benchmarks such as URLB or ExoRL may obscure representation-specific limitations, motivating the development of dedicated benchmarks.

papers.title: Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning Under Partial Observability
papers.abstract: Recent work has shown that, under certain assumptions, zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL) methods can generalise to any unseen task in an environment after reward-free pre-training. Access to Markov states is one such assumption, yet, in many real-world applications, the Markov state is only partially observable. Here, we explore how the performance of standard zero-shot RL methods degrades when subjected to partially observability, and show that, as in single-task RL, memory-based architectures are an effective remedy. We evaluate our memory-based zero-shot RL methods in domains where the states, rewards and a change in dynamics are partially observed, and show improved performance over memory-free baselines. Our code is open-sourced via: https://enjeeneer.io/projects/bfms-with-memory/.
