We report the mean and standard deviation across three runs for the policy learning module, each with 200 evaluation episodes, for three key evaluation metrics: episode target hit, episode goal hit, and episode reward. The target hit metric indicates whether the target ball moved, while the goal hit metric reflects whether the goal was reached. 5.2 Implementation Details We utilize the gco and g implementations provided in, along with the HVAE implementation from, with an action embedding size of 128. The message passing function gre consists of two Graph Convolution Network layers, each followed by a ReLU activation function. The sparsity threshold (ϵ) of the action observation adjacency matrix A is set to 0.95. The action observation classifier ρ is composed of two fully connected layers, each followed by a ReLU activation function. The contrastive loss Lcont uses a temperature value of κ = 0.5, a negative observation set size of K′ = 5, and a hyper-parameter λcont with a value of 1e−1. The hyper-parameter λce for the observation classification loss is set to 1e−3. The action representation learning module is trained using the RAdam optimizer with a learning rate of 1e−3, over 10,000 epochs, and a batch size of K = 32. For the policy learning module, we adopt the implementations of the state encoder, utility function, and auxiliary function from. We utilize the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) method to learn the policy function π, and extend the specific PPO implementation from. The number of sampled actions is set to K = 50 and the maximum episode length is set to 30 timesteps. The mixing rate λ for generating augmented actions representations is sampled from a Beta(0.4, 0.4) distribution. The policy is trained using the Adam optimizer with a learning rate of 1e−3 for 6e7 steps and a batch size of 3,072. The entropy coefficient β is set to 5e−3. 5.3 Comparison Results We evaluate the performance of our AGLO framework on the zero-shot action generalization problem with limited action observations. Specifically, we conduct experiments using three different numbers of observations per action: 5, 7 and 9 observations. These correspond to 10%, 15% and 20% of the observations per action used in prior work. We compare our AGLO against two zero-shot action generalization methods: Hierarchical Variational Auto-Encoder (HVAE) and Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). The comparison results for the Push, Navigate and Obstacle tasks are presented in Table 1. Table 1 shows that our AGLO framework consistently and significantly outperforms both the VAE and HVAE methods across all three tasks, for all three numbers of action observations, and across all evaluation metrics. The performance improvements on the Push task are substantial, with gains exceeding 23%, 25% and 17% in terms of Target Hit, and 18%, 17% and 15% in terms of Goal Hit for 5, 7 and 9 action observations, respectively. Moreover, AGLO demonstrates superior performance in terms of average rewards collected on the Push task, achieving remarkable improvements of approximately 1.99 (248% relative gain), 1.84 (317% relative gain) and 1.56 (162% relative gain) with 5, 7 and 9 action observations, respectively. The performance gains on the more challenging Navigate and Obstacle tasks are even more pronounced, where both VAE and HVAE struggle to learn generalizable policies. On the Navigate task, AGLO achieves significant gains in terms of Target Hit with improvements of around 32%, 42% and 42% for 5, 7 and 9 observations, respectively. Similarly, on the Obstacle task, AGLO outperforms both VAE and HAVE in terms of Target Hit by 35%, 33% and 25% for 5, 7 and 9 action observations, respectively. These results highlight the superior performance of our framework compared to existing zero-shot action generalization methods, particularly in scenarios where the number of available action observations is limited, across three challenging sequential decision-making tasks. 5.4 Ablation Study We conducted an ablation study to investigate the contributions of three novel components in our framework: the observation action classification loss Lce and the action observation contrastive learning loss Lcont in the action representation learning module, as well as the action representation augmentation (denoted as Action Aug.) in the policy learning module. Specifically, we consider five variants of our proposed AGLO framework, where in each variant we remove one or two of the three novel components. The evaluation is carried out on the CREATE Push task with 5 observations per action, and the results are presented in Table 2. The results in Table 2 demonstrate performance degradations in all variants across the three evaluation metrics compared to the full proposed framework. The significant performance drops are observed in variants that do not include action representation augmentation, highlighting the critical role of action representation augmentation in improving the generalization of the learned policy. Moreover, the notable performance drops when Lcont and Lce are removed underscore the importance of both of these losses in learning discriminative and cohesive action representations, particularly as reflected in the reward and goal hit metrics. The consistent performance degradations across all metrics for all variants highlight the essential contribution of each novel component in our proposed framework. 5.5 Analysis of Policy Learning We also investigate the dynamics of the policy learning process within our AGLO framework. Specifically, we sample 200 training and 200 testing episodes, where the actions in the training episodes are drawn from the set of training actions, and the actions in the testing episodes are drawn from the set of testing actions. We evaluate the performance of our framework on both sets of episodes throughout the policy learning process by measuring the mean and standard deviation of Target hit and collected rewards across three runs. To assess its robustness, we compare the performance of our AGLO framework against both VAE and HVAE methods on the Push task with 5 and 7 observations per action, Table 2: Ablation study results (standard deviation within brackets) on the Push task in the CREATE environment with 5 observations per action. Figure 2 demonstrates that while all three methods perform similarly in the early stage of policy learning, the performance of AGLO framework diverges significantly from that of VAE and HVAE as learning progresses. In particular, AGLO exhibits steady and consistent improvement in terms of both rewards and Target hit metrics as the number of environment steps increases, across both numbers of action observations. This improvement is observed in both the training and testing episodes, highlighting that our framework effectively learns stable and generalizable policies that perform well on both seen and unseen actions. In contrast, HVAE and VAE methods either converge to suboptimal policy solutions—indicative of a lack of exploration during learning—or develop unstable policies where performance fluctuates or drops significantly during policy learning. Our AGLO framework also exhibits smaller standard deviations across different runs compared to both the HVAE and VAE methods, highlighting the robustness of its training process. These results underscore the superior performance of AGLO in learning stable policies that generalize well to unseen actions, while also highlighting the limitations of current methods. CONCLUSION In this paper, we introduced a novel AGLO framework to tackle the challenging problem of zero-shot action generalization in Reinforcement Learning, specifically targeting scenarios with limited action observations. Our proposed framework consists of two key components: an action representation learning module and a policy learning module. The action representation learning module encodes the limited set of action observations to generate representative action embeddings. The policy learning module then leverages the learned action embeddings to augment the representations of seen actions with synthetic action representations. The policy is subsequently trained on both the original rep- (a) 5 Observations, Target Hit (b) 5 Observations, Reward (c) 7 Observations, Target Hit (d) 7 Observations, Reward Figure 2: Policy learning analysis of VAE, HVAE and our AGLO on the Push task, with 5 and 7 observations per action, evaluated using the Target hit and reward metrics. resentations of seen actions and their synthetic counterparts, enabling the learning of a policy that generalizes effectively to unseen actions. papers.title: Sensor-Layout-Agnostic Navigation via Geometric Observation Canonicalization
papers.abstract: Existing visual navigation policies are inherently bound to fixed camera configurations, creating a fundamental barrier to zero-shot deployment across heterogeneous robot sensor layouts. To overcome this limitation, we present an embodiment-informed navigation policy capable of generalizing across diverse depth sensor configurations on a specific aerial platform. Instead of implicitly learning spatial alignments, our approach explicitly unprojects depth measurements from arbitrary depth sensor payloads, varying in sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and intrinsics, into a shared robot-centric frame, stitching them into a unified spherical range image and a binary validity mask. This mask allows the downstream policy to explicitly distinguish covered space from unobserved blind spots. Trained via reinforcement learning with aggressive camera randomization, our policy generalizes zero-shot to unseen layouts featuring up to seven cameras, scaling success rates from 78% to 95% as total spatial sensing coverage increases. Finally, real-world flight trials on a physical quadrotor, conducted in an obstacle-filled corridor and an outdoor forest, validate the policy's zero-shot transfer across camera configurations and its resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts.

papers.full_text: Existing visual navigation policies are inherently bound to fixed camera configurations, creating a fundamental barrier to zero-shot deployment across heterogeneous robot sensor layouts. To overcome this limitation, we present an embodiment-informed navigation policy capable of generalizing across diverse depth sensor configurations on a specific aerial platform. Instead of implicitly learning spatial alignments, our approach explicitly unprojects depth measurements from arbitrary depth sensor payloads, varying in sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and intrinsics, into a shared robot-centric frame, stitching them into a unified spherical range image and a binary validity mask. This mask allows the downstream policy to explicitly distinguish covered space from unobserved blind spots. Trained via reinforcement learning with aggressive camera randomization, our policy generalizes zero-shot to unseen layouts featuring up to seven cameras, scaling success rates from 78% to 95% as total spatial sensing coverage increases. Finally, real-world flight trials on a physical quadrotor, conducted in an obstacle-filled corridor and an outdoor forest, validate the policy’s zero-shot transfer across camera configurations and its resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts. I. INTRODUCTION Deploying diverse autonomous robots across unstructured environments often requires custom tuning or re-training policies whenever sensor hardware changes. Consequently, zero-shot generalist policies are essential to eliminate perplatform engineering and enable seamless deployment across diverse, evolving robot fleets. To navigate reliably, a generalist policy must ingest raw sensor information observations and map them directly to control commands across highly diverse embodiments. A major barrier to this generalization is that navigation policies are historically bound to specific camera configurations and vehicle frames –. This tight coupling means even minor adjustments to the sensor payload, such as varying mounting heights, altering pitch angles, or integrating auxiliary cameras, render the policy unusable, traditionally demanding expensive network retraining. Recent research has progressed significantly on generalizing policies to robots with different dynamic responses – and kinematic chains,. However, existing visual generalists either suffer from high computational latency or rely on simplified geometric assumptions, thereby preventing lightweight, real-time 3D navigation across heterogeneous camera layouts. In this work, we address the problem of reactive local collision avoidance for a broad family of multi- The authors are with the Norwegian Institute of Science and Technology, Norway. {welf.rehberg, konstantinos.alexis}@ntnu.no This work was supported by the Horizon Europe Grant Agreement No. 101119774, the Research Council of Norway under Award NO-357451 and the NVIDIA Academic Grant Program using NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Max-Q and A100 GPU-Hours on Saturn Cloud. Deployment Simulation Navigation Generalist Fig. 1: Overview of the navigation generalist method. sensor depth camera setups on a fixed dynamical system. Rather than forcing the neural network to implicitly associate visual coordinates with motion primitives, we inject a strong geometric prior into the network’s perception pipeline. We unproject exteroceptive depth measurements from a variable number of arbitrary sensors and map them into a shared, unified egocentric spherical coordinate system, yielding a range image and an associated binary validity mask expressed in the robot’s base coordinate frame. Canonicalization projects all sensor measurements into a common coordinate system, removing the need for the policy to implicitly learn sensorto-body frame alignments. An overview of the method is shown in Fig. 1. Through extensive simulated evaluations and real-world quadrotor deployments, we demonstrate that our embodiment-informed policy achieves robust, zero-shot transfer across highly heterogeneous exteroceptive configurations and environments and is robust to sensor dropouts on systems with redundant sensor configurations. Specifically, the contributions of this paper are four-fold: • We introduce an exteroceptive canonicalization pipeline that maps arbitrary depth feeds to a unified, egocentric spherical range tensor and a binary validity mask, enabling generalization to sensor count, mounting extrinsics, and sensor intrinsics. • We present a reactive navigation policy trained via reinforcement learning under aggressive sensor extrinsics and intrinsics randomization, eliminating the need to implicitly learn sensor-body-coordinate alignments. • We demonstrate zero-shot generalization in simulation to out-of-distribution (OOD) layouts featuring up to seven cameras, achieving navigation performance comparable to specialized, layout-specific policies. • We validate our approach on a physical quadrotor across different sensor configurations navigating cluttered indoor corridors and dense forests, demonstrating robust real-world zero-shot transfer and resilience to sudden online sensor dropouts. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews prior work on generalist navigation and crossembodiment learning. Section III introduces the problem formulation. Section IV details the system family considered in this work, the geometric observation canonicalization method, our architecture choices, and our training setup. Section V presents our ablation studies, simulation benchmarks, and real-world flight deployments. Finally, Section VI concludes the paper and discusses future research directions. II. RELATED WORK Within the domain of cross-embodiment control, existing research predominantly focuses on adapting low-level motor or joint commands to variations in physical dynamics, such as mass, inertia, and joint kinematics –. However, this body of work leaves the challenge of exteroceptive perception geometry largely unaddressed, assuming static or platform-specific sensor arrangements. Recently, extending generalization capabilities to visual navigation has gained significant momentum. Frameworks such as GNM,, and enable generalized navigation across diverse physical embodiments, spanning mobile robots, quadrupeds, and aerial vehicles. Despite their success, these architectures operate under a restrictive assumption: they assume a fixed nominal sensor payload per platform, most commonly a single forward-facing camera. While these models implicitly absorb minor camera height or pitch variations that are present across large training datasets, they lack explicit mechanisms to handle multi-camera setups, arbitrary 3D mounting extrinsics, or variable sensor counts. While X- Nav targets hardware-agnosticism by deterministically projecting depth images into a 1D laser scan format, their training pipeline and evaluation are restricted to a single nominal camera configuration with a 90◦ field of view (FOV). Consequently, the policy is never exposed during training to vastly different camera poses, different camera intrinsics, multi-camera setups, or unobserved spatial gaps. Furthermore, reducing depth observations to a 1D horizontal representation fundamentally restricts the system to a 2D plane, precluding its application to 3D aerial flight where elevation-aware obstacle avoidance is essential. Generalist vision-language-action (VLA) navigators, incorporate multi-view visual feeds by scaling up highcapacity visual transformers to associate RGB tokens with high-level semantic subgoals. However, these models target low-frequency planning rather than local collision avoidance and suffer from high computational latency ( [13] requiring off-board GPU infrastructure), making them incapable of the high-frequency control loops needed for real-time onboard flight in cluttered environments. Additionally, the work in [12] severely limits the number of sensors (max 2) and assumes that one sensor faces strictly forward, while accommodates up to 8 cameras but randomizes only mounting height and horizontal FOV continuously, selecting the underlying sensor layout from 6 predefined discrete configurations. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a single generalist policy for real-time, onboard 3D reactive collision avoidance across heterogeneous sensor layouts. Rather than relying on heavy transformer backbones or predefined sensor configurations, our lightweight model runs onboard embedded hardware, operating zero-shot across arbitrary sensor counts, extrinsics, and intrinsics. By unprojecting arbitrary depth feeds into an egocentric spherical range tensor paired with a binary validity mask, we decouple policy execution from viewpoint alignment. Trained across wide continuous variations in camera counts, 3D mounting extrinsics and sensor intrinsics, our policy architecture learns to reason over visibility and obstacle proximity, achieving robust zeroshot OOD transfer and online fault tolerance on physical hardware. III. PROBLEM FORMULATION We consider the problem of generalizing a single navigation policy across a family of systems characterized by their morphology vectors γ ∈ Γ, where Γ denotes the considered family of systems. We formulate this problem as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP), where the policy must -for a single dynamical system- generalize across varying depth camera setups and incorporate observations from up to ncam arbitrarily placed and oriented depth sensors while navigating tight, cluttered environments. The morphology vector is defined by the corresponding sensor extrinsics BT Cj and intrinsics Kj as γ = [vec([BT C1,..., BT Cncam]), vec([K1,..., Kncam])]. (1) Here, B denotes the body frame of the robot and Cj denotes the coordinate frame of sensor j and vec(·) denotes the vectorize operation. Given a 3D start position ps ∈ R3 and a goal position pg ∈ R3, both expressed in the inertial frame I, the objective is to generate a sequence of actions at = [at,x, at,y, at,z, at,ω] with the first three components being linear reference velocities and at,ω being the reference yaw rate, all expressed in the body frame B. At each timestep t, the policy has access only to (a) a proprioceptive state estimate xt = [g⊤ t, ξt, ηt, v⊤ t, ω⊤ t ]⊤ ∈ R12, where gt = [ˆd ⊤ t, dt]⊤ ∈ R4 concatenates the unit direction ˆdt ∈ R3 from the robot to the goal and the Euclidean goal distance dt ∈ R, both expressed in B; ξt, ηt ∈ R denote the roll and pitch angles; and vt, ωt ∈ R3 are the linear and angular velocities expressed in B; (b) the previous action at−1; and (c) the depth observations dj(u, v) (axial), with j ∈ 1,..., ncam, together with the sensor extrinsics BT Cj and intrinsics Kj. IV. METHOD A. System Family The family of systems to which the policy is expected to generalize to is created by sampling configurations in the following manner. For a fixed multirotor system, the number of cameras is uniformly sampled from the set {1,..., ncam} (ncam = 4 in this work). The camera extrinsics are randomized as follows. The position of camera j in the body frame, BtCj, is sampled uniformly from a box enclosing the full robot, with bounds detailed in Table I. The orientation of camera j in the body frame, BRCj, is restricted to configurations favorable for navigation, excluding cameras oriented fully upward or downward as illustrated in Fig. 2 and uniformly sampled from the ranges detailed in Table I. The camera intrinsics Kj are randomized by uniformly sampling the focal length f, the horizontal aperture ah, and the aperture aspect ratio ρa = ah/av from the ranges detailed in Table I. Where av is the vertical aperture. The resulting FOV ranges from [50◦, 131◦] in azimuth and [26◦, 142◦] in elevation. Note that the image resolution during training is fixed, but as described in Section IV-B resampling the real image to the target resolution used in training lets us deploy cameras with varying resolutions. Observation Canonicalization 1) Canonicalized Spherical Range Image To enable the policy to operate on sensor readings obtained from arbitrarily placed cameras, we transform the obtained depth scans dj(u, v) (j ∈ {1,.., ncam}) into patches in a spherical range image r(iϕ, iθ). The resulting point cloud is binned into a 2D spherical range image r(iϕ, iθ). When multiple points fall into the same bin the one with the smallest distance is chosen. Training 1) Reward Design For each state transition, the agent receives a scalar reward Rt composed of terms that encourage goal progress, collision avoidance, and visibility-aligned motion, while regularizing action magnitudes and rate of change. The first group of terms encourages goal-directed motion. Let pI denote the current positions expressed in the inertial frame. Two position-based rewards with different spatial scales are used d2 g = ��pg − pI ��2 2, rgi = exp � − d2 g σ2gi �, i ∈ {1, 2}, (7) where σgi are parameters defining the width of the kernel function. The smaller value of σg2 makes rg2 more sensitive to the distance near the goal and therefore places greater emphasis on accurate goal tracking. Goal progress is further incentivized by aligning inertial linear velocity vI with the target direction rv = � vI, pg − pI ∥pg − pI∥2 + ϵ �, (8) where ϵ > 0 prevents division by zero. To encourage the commanded linear velocity ax,y,z (linear velocity component of action at) toward observed space (Fig. 4), rd = ∥ax,y,z∥2q(ax,y,z) scales action magnitude by the valid bin fraction q(ax,y,z) = |W| � (iϕ,iθ)∈W(ax,y,z) m(iϕ, iθ), (9) where m(iϕ, iθ) ∈ {0, 1} is the validity mask, and W(ax,y,z) is an ncb × ncb angular window of cardinality |W| centered on the commanded velocity direction. To penalize motion toward nearby obstacles, a time-to-collision (TTC) penalty rc is computed across the range grid. The closing speed along each bin’s unit ray direction ˆn(iϕ, iθ) is s(iϕ, iθ) = vT B ˆn(iϕ, iθ), where vB is the body-frame velocity. A bin contributes to the TTC calculation only if it contains a valid measurement and the robot is moving toward the corresponding direction. Dropping bin indices for brevity, per-bin TTC is defined as tc =    r max(s, ϵ), if s > 0 and m = 1, tcmax, otherwise, (10) where r is range, m ∈ {0, 1} is validity, ϵ > 0 prevents division by small speeds, and tcmax bounds invalid or nonapproaching (s ≤ 0) bins. The minimum predicted TTC across all bins determines the penalty tcmin = min iϕ,iθ tc(iϕ, iθ), rc = − exp � −βct2 cmin �, (11) where βc > 0 is a kernel scaling parameter. The reward further penalizes collisions and undesirable changes in the commanded actions. A collision that terminates an episode incurs the penalty rt = −1 and rt = 0 otherwise. To discourage abrupt changes in the commanded action and unnecessarily large commands, the action-rate and actionmagnitude penalties are defined as rr = −∥at − at−1∥2 2, rm = −∥at∥2 2. (12) The individual reward terms are combined into the final scalar reward according to R(st, at) = αcurr (αg1rg1 + αg2rg2 + αvrv) + αdrd + αcrc + αtrt + αrrr + αmrm, (13) where α□ denotes tunable weights. In addition to the reward design, an auxiliary reconstruction objective is used during training to encourage the depth encoder to retain information about the observed regions. A decoder block ψdec reconstructs the canonicalized range image and validity mask from the latent depth feature fdepth. The range reconstruction loss is defined as Lr = ∥m ⊙ (¯r − r)∥2 F ∥m∥1, (14) where ¯r denotes the reconstructed range image, ∥·∥F denotes the Frobenius norm, and ⊙ denotes element-wise multiplication. The validity mask restricts the range reconstruction loss to bins containing valid measurements. The reconstruction of the validity mask is guided via a binary cross-entropy loss Lm = − 1 N � � m ⊙ log( ¯m) + (1 − m) ⊙ log(1 − ¯m) �, (15) Fig. 4: Actions in observed region. ����� ������ Fig. 5: Example of a randomly generated obstacle-filled environment. where ¯m denotes the predicted probability of validity and N is the total number of bins in the validity mask. The total loss used to optimize the network weights is then given by L = LPPO + αL (Lr + Lm), (16) where LPPO denotes the Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) loss used to optimize the policy and value networks, and αL determines the relative contribution of the reconstruction losses. 2) Environment Setup The training environment consists of a closed room populated with obstacles shown in Fig. 5. The obstacles are placed randomly within the room, with their positions and orientations randomized upon each environment reset. A diverse set of obstacle geometries and sizes is used, ranging from small, thin objects to large, flat panels. The number of obstacles is controlled using a performance-based curriculum: the obstacle density is increased when the policy is able to reliably reach the goal at the current difficulty level. Upon reset a random number of depth cameras is uniformly sampled within the bounds described in Section IV-A. The initial position, orientation and velocities of the robot, as well as the goal position, are randomized at the beginning of each episode. To facilitate sim-to-real transfer, a stereo-depth noise model similar to that of is applied to the depth images generated during training. Moreover, the parameters of the low-level geometric velocity controller are randomized at each environment reset to improve robustness to variations in the system dynamics encountered in the real-world. V. EVALUATION To evaluate the proposed generalist navigation policy, we conduct a series of simulation and real-world experiments alongside ablation studies. The policy is trained using our described methodology on a workstation equipped with a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU and an Intel Xeon w7-3565X CPU for a total of 1.9 × 106 environment steps. We utilize Isaac for GPU-accelerated physics simulation and environment management, which interfaces with the SKRL library to leverage its implementation of PPO. To evaluate a policy we run 1000 episodes, resampling both the system configuration and the obstacle layout upon every reset. Throughout these trials, we maintain the simulation curriculum at maximum difficulty, resulting in environments consistently populated by 37 randomly placed obstacles. We report crash rate (CR) and success rate (SR). An episode is considered crashed if a collision occurs and considered successful if it reaches the goal position within 1m radius. A. Ablation Studies We conduct ablation studies to evaluate the individual contributions of our two primary architectural design choices: the binary validity mask and the auxiliary masked reconstruction loss. Specifically, we evaluate two baseline versions of our method: (i) completely omitting the validity mask from the policy input and also the masked reconstruction loss (denoted as w/o mask & rec. loss). Specifically this means m, Lr and Lm are removed. (ii) providing the validity mask to the network but disabling the guiding auxiliary masked reconstruction loss (denoted as w/o rec. loss). Specifically this means Lr and Lm are removed. Note that in both cases m is still used in the reward calculation. The quantitative results summarized in Table II demonstrate that both components are critical to the policy’s performance, providing complementary contributions that reduce the CR and maximize the overall SR over the full training population. Fig. 6 shows that adding these two components significantly increases sample efficiency and stability of the training process. B. Simulation Results We evaluate our generalist navigation policy in simulation across the entire family of system configurations considered in this work. 1) Performance Evaluation To isolate the influence of sensor redundancy, we evaluate the performance for each camera count separately. Notably, we also test the policy on configurations with 5, 6, and 7 cameras; since these layouts are entirely unseen during training, they serve as a rigorous evaluation of the policy’s zero-shot generalization to OOD sensor numbers. Table III presents the results of this evaluation. As the number of cameras increases, the CR decreases and the SR increases until performance eventually plateaus. We hypothesize that this trend is driven by the expansion of the combined FOV; as more cameras are integrated, the aggregate angular coverage (number of bins covered by a sensor divided by total number of bins) increases until additional sensors no longer provide the policy with novel or actionable information about the surrounding environment. 2) Comparison to Specialist Policies We further compare the performance of our generalist policy against two classes of specialized baselines: Comparison with Single-Configuration Specialists: First, we compare our generalist policy against configurationspecific specialists trained using our identical methodology, but restricted to a single, fixed camera setup throughout training (i.e., without camera randomization on reset). We sample two random configurations for each camera count (1,..., 4), yielding eight distinct configurations for evaluation. The t-SNE visualization of the camera-configuration parameter space is shown as triangles (▲) in the t-SNE visualization (Fig. 10). All specialist policies are trained until convergence. The quantitative results, averaged across all eight configurations, are presented in Table IV. Our generalist policy exhibits a performance penalty of only a 2% increase in CR and a 2% decrease in SR compared to the specialists, despite being trained to generalize across the entire system family. Comparison with State-of-the-Art Single-Camera Specialist: Second, we compare our method against a state of the art (SOTA) reinforcement learning architecture tailored specifically for single-camera quadrotor navigation. To build a comprehensive evaluation set, we sample four additional single-camera configurations, which, combined with the two configurations from our previous evaluation, result in six single-camera test setups. This evaluation set explicitly includes the original, nominal camera configuration used in [17] (0◦ pitch and forward facing camera). These configurations are represented as circles in the t-SNE embedding (Fig. 10). We selected the baseline architecture from [17] because it was developed and demonstrated in a similar obstacle layout. To ensure a fair and rigorous comparison in simulation, we replace their depth encoder, which was partially pre-trained on real-world images, with a standard convolutional neural network trained entirely end-to-end alongside the policy in simulation. Empirically, this modification yielded superior simulation performance compared to using the original pre-trained weights. The specialist policies are trained until convergence again. The results averaged over all six configurations are summarized in Table V. The evaluation demonstrates that our generalist policy performs on par with this highly specialized architecture. Additionally, we compare our approach against the reported CR and SR in [18] (Table 7, Line 24), which evaluates a system with a forward-facing camera with 0◦ pitch, a wide FOV (130◦) for a reference velocity of 1 m/s in an environment closely matching ours. While both methods achieve a comparable SR, their reported CR is 6% lower. This comparison is approximate because the reported results in [18] were obtained under a different implementation/environment. This reduced crash rate is likely attributable to their explicit FOV constraints, which constrain the commanded velocity vector to lie within the camera frustum. 3) Design Space Evaluation To visualize policy performance across a dense design space, we evaluate two-camera configurations sweeping TABLE IV: Evaluation of our generalist against specialist policies (our method). ▲ Generalist Specialist CR 0.05 0.03 SR 0.93 0.95 TABLE V: Evaluation of our generalist against specialist policies trained with a modified version of the architecture in [17]. As camera pitch diverges from the body’s x−y plane, CR increases and SR decreases. This stems from underactuated quadrotor dynamics, where attitude pitch is rigidly coupled to horizontal acceleration: non-zero mounting offsets force continuous attitude adjustments to align view axes with the velocity vector. Performance also degrades at extreme relative yaw angles due to either redundant FOV overlap (narrow yaw) or loss of forward-flight coverage (at extreme wide yaw angles, the cameras point in opposite directions). 4) Sensitivity Analysis To evaluate how mismatches between the estimated embodiment parameters and the platform’s true physical parameters affect policy performance, we conduct a sensitivity analysis. Specifically, we track the evolution of the CR and SR as perturbations of increasing magnitude are applied to the system parameters used to compute the canonicalized range image and the validity mask. Perturbation magnitudes are defined as a percentage of each parameter’s randomization range (see Table I), and the sign of each disturbance is sampled with equal probability. The resulting CR and SR curves are shown in Fig. 8. The analysis indicates no performance drop for parameter mismatches of up to 10% of the randomization range for all intrinsic parameters and for the camera position. For camera orientation, the method remains robust to yaw mismatches of up to 2.5% and to roll and pitch mismatches of up to 7.5% of their respective randomization ranges. These results highlight the robustness of the proposed approach and support its suitability for simto-real transfer. Note that the parameter vector γ is zero padded to unify different camera numbers. C. Real-World Experiments To validate the real-world performance of our generalized navigation policy, we first deploy it on a custom quadrotor platform equipped with three Intel RealSense D455 depth cameras, an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX onboard computer, a Texas Instruments IWR6843AOP-EVM radar, and a Pixracer Pro flight controller running the PX4 autopilot firmware. State estimation is resolved onboard using Radar Inertial Odometry (RIO), and low-level velocity tracking commands are executed directly by the PX4 controller. Our policy runs entirely onboard, performing inference at 10 Hz. The three cameras are physically arranged as illustrated in Fig. 9. By selectively disabling individual camera streams, we construct three distinct hardware configurations to evaluate zero-shot adaptation: (i) all three cameras active, (ii) cameras 1 and 2 active, and (iii) only camera 3 active. The t-SNE visualization of the camera-configuration parameter space is visualized in the t-SNE embedding in Fig. 10 (indicated by the stars ). We evaluate the system across two highly distinct real-world environments: a cluttered indoor corridor and a dense forest. 1) Cluttered Hallway First, we evaluate the generalist policy across all three sensor configurations in an indoor hallway cluttered with obstacle panels, with vertical (z) actions constrained to prevent flying over obstacles (Fig. 11 a)). When initialized with its single active camera pointing away from the goal, the policy demonstrates safety-first behavior: rather than translating blindly into unobserved space, it executes an inplace yaw rotation to align its camera with the target before initiating forward movement. In all environments, the policy smoothly avoids the obstacles in its way. Robustness to Sensor Dropout: Additionally, we evaluate policy robustness under online sensor dropout. For this we first re-run the 2-, 3-, and 4-camera experiments in simulation while randomly disabling one active sensor mid-episode (removing the depth readings from the canonicalized observations and setting the corresponding mask pixels to 0). Despite the sudden loss of sensor coverage, the policy adapts online in most of the cases: 2-camera setups achieve a CR of 0.15 and SR 0.74, 3- camera setups reach a CR of 0.10 and SR 0.85, and 4-camera setups achieve a CR of 0.05 and SR 0.92. We also demonstrate dropout robustness in two real-world scenarios (Fig. 11 b)). In the first, camera 3 abruptly fails mid-trajectory on a three-camera setup. In the second, camera 1 is disabled midflight while camera 3, pointing in the opposite direction, is simultaneously activated, instantaneously reversing the sensing envelope. The policy handles this shift safely: it immediately halts forward translation, executes a ∼ 180◦ yaw rotation to align the newly active camera with the target, and resumes navigation. Generalization to Different Depth Sensors: To demonstrate our methods capacity to generalize across heterogeneous depth-sensing hardware in reality, we replace camera 2 (Intel RealSense D455) with a pmd flexx2 Time-of-Flight (ToF) sensor at the identical physical mounting position. This ToF sensor features a significantly narrower FOV (56◦×44◦) compared to the D455 (87◦×58◦). We conduct an experiment utilizing a heterogeneous sensor setup consisting of the newly integrated pmd flexx2 and camera 1 (D455) (t-SNE embedding shown in Fig. 10). The successful navigation of the platform shown in Fig. 11 d) demonstrates that our canonicalization pipeline effectively adapts to varying sensor models, physical resolutions, and fields of view without requiring retraining. 2) Forest To evaluate the policy’s zero-shot generalization to OOD geometric structures, we deployed our system in a dense natural forest. Note that we remove the constraint on the z-velocity in this environment. Unlike the primitive, geometric obstacles (e.g., cylinders and planar barriers) encountered during simulation training, natural forest environments present highly complex, non-convex topologies characterized by thin tree trunks, overhanging branches, and irregular foliage. Operating entirely without fine-tuning, our generalist policy successfully navigates this challenging environment. As illustrated in Fig. 11 c), the policy leverages multiple sensor streams to navigate around unobserved spatial regions and thin obstacles, executing smooth, continuous 3D avoidance maneuvers while maintaining target forward progress. VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK In this work, we presented a camera-layout-agnostic policy for reactive local collision avoidance across heterogeneous depth sensor configurations. By unprojecting depth measurements into a canonical egocentric spherical range image paired with a binary validity mask, our approach eliminates the need to implicitly learn camera alignment, enabling zeroshot adaptation to varying camera counts, extrinsics, and intrinsics. Simulation evaluations confirmed zero-shot generalization to OOD sensor payloads with up to seven cameras. Physical quadrotor flight trials in cluttered indoor corridors and dense forests demonstrated robustness to complex geometries and resilience to sudden online camera dropouts. Future work will couple this exteroceptive canonicalization with morphology-aware dynamics to achieve joint transfer across both sensor layouts and physical robot platforms. REFERENCES A. papers.title: Test-Time Adaptation with CLIP Reward for Zero-Shot Generalization in Vision-Language Models
papers.abstract: One fascinating aspect of pre-trained vision-language models~(VLMs) learning under language supervision is their impressive zero-shot generalization capability. However, this ability is hindered by distribution shifts between the training and testing data. Previous test time adaptation~(TTA) methods for VLMs in zero-shot classification rely on minimizing the entropy of model outputs, tending to be stuck in incorrect model predictions. In this work, we propose TTA with feedback to rectify the model output and prevent the model from becoming blindly confident. Specifically, a CLIP model is adopted as the reward model during TTA and provides feedback for the VLM. Given a single test sample, the VLM is forced to maximize the CLIP reward between the input and sampled results from the VLM output distribution. The proposed framework is highly flexible and universal. Beyond the classification task, with task-specific sampling strategies and a proper reward baseline choice, RLCF can be easily extended to not only discrimination tasks like retrieval but also generalization tasks like image captioning, improving the zero-shot generalization capacity of VLMs. According to the characteristics of these VL tasks, we build different fully TTA pipelines with RLCF to improve the zero-shot generalization ability of various VLMs. Extensive experiments along with promising empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of RLCF. The code is available at https://github.com/mzhaoshuai/RLCF.

papers.full_text: One fascinating aspect of pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) learning under language supervision is their impressive zero-shot generalization capability. However, this ability is hindered by distribution shifts between the training and testing data. Previous test time adaptation (TTA) methods for VLMs in zeroshot classification rely on minimizing the entropy of model outputs, tending to be stuck in incorrect model predictions. In this work, we propose TTA with feedback to rectify the model output and prevent the model from becoming blindly confident. Specifically, a CLIP model is adopted as the reward model during TTA and provides feedback for the VLM. Given a single test sample, the VLM is forced to maximize the CLIP reward between the input and sampled results from the VLM output distribution. The proposed reinforcement learning with CLIP feedback (RLCF) framework is highly flexible and universal. Beyond the classification task, with task-specific sampling strategies and a proper reward baseline choice, RLCF can be easily extended to not only discrimination tasks like retrieval but also generalization tasks like image captioning, improving the zero-shot generalization capacity of VLMs. According to the characteristics of these VL tasks, we build different fully TTA pipelines with RLCF to improve the zero-shot generalization ability of various VLMs. Extensive experiments along with promising empirical results demonstrate the effectiveness of RLCF. The code is available at INTRODUCTION Pre-trained vision-language models (VLMs) learning under language supervision (Radford et al., 2021; Jia et al., 2021; Yuan et al., 2021) exhibit promising zero-shot transferability. This encourages researchers to explore the capabilities of VLMs across a number of tasks in a zero-shot fashion. For example, employ CLIP for zero-shot text-driven avatar generation, adapt CLIP for zero-shot sketch-based image retrieval, and achieve zero-shot image captioning without images. Nonetheless, the large domain gap between training and test data is still challenging for VLMs in a zero-shot circumstance. In this work, we investigate how to fulfill the domain gap during test time in various tasks without task-specific training corpus, namely, test time adaptation (TTA) for VLMs with a zero-shot prerequisite. One pioneer TTA work in improving the zero-shot classification ability of VLMs is test time prompt tuning (TPT). Given a single test sample, TPT optimizes the learnable prefix tokens by minimizing the entropy of model outputs to bootstrap its generalization capacity. Nevertheless, making the model confident in its predictions is a double-edged sword. It does reduce the test error and close the domain gap at a certain level, but it makes the model stick to its incorrect predictions and unable to get out of the dilemma by itself as shown in the top of Figure 1a. Entropy minimization tends to make the model blindly confident. ∗Part of this work is done during an internship at Baidu Inc. Yi Yang is the corresponding author. Figure 1: Feedback mechanism in zero-shot generalization with CLIP as the reward model. Inspired by the success of the feedback mechanism in language and vision tasks (Ouyang et al., 2022; OpenAI, 2023; Pinto et al., 2023), we introduce feedback during test time to rectify the VLM output as shown in the bottom of Figure 1a. Previous feedback methods leverage labeled preference data to train a reward model (Ouyang et al., 2022; Lee et al., 2023) or use labels to calculate the reward (Cho et al., 2022; Pinto et al., 2023). Without ground truth, we refer to the well-recognized CLIP model as the feedback resource. CLIP shows powerful generalization capacity across many VL tasks. The outputs of CLIP are also well-calibrated (without fine-tuning on a specific dataset), i.e., the score from CLIP accurately reflects its uncertainty about the input sample. This makes CLIP a reliable reward model. One more question is why feedback rather than directly tuning with CLIP supervision? demonstrate that model learning with feedback has better generalization abilities than a supervised fine-tuning model. We get the same conclusion from our empirical results. Furthermore, CLIP supervision cannot be directly used in generation tasks like image captioning, while the feedback mechanism is versatile. Our proposed framework, coined as reinforcement learning with CLIP feedback (RLCF), is flexible and universal for TTA with different VLMs in various tasks. With task-specific sampling strategies and a proper reward baseline choice, RLCF is applicable across zero-shot classification, text-image retrieval, and image captioning. In these tasks, the model is given a single test sample, we then sample K candidates from the output distribution. For discrimination tasks like classification and retrieval, the top-K sampling is applied; for the caption generalization task, a beam search method is adopted. Assuming the input is an image, like Figure 1b, the CLIP model first gives the CLIP- Score between the image and all candidate sentences. As CLIPScore is always non-negative, the average score is subtracted from the calculated scores. This average baseline aims to distinguish which model behaviors are encouraged and which are discouraged. Then the learnable parameters in the TTA model are optimized by REINFORCE algorithm. While the reward design and learning algorithm remain consistent across various tasks, the TTA pipelines are tailored to each specific task. For classification, we inherit the data augmentation and confidence selection pipeline from TPT, making it work for not only prefix tuning but also backbone adaptation. For retrieval, considering a large number of candidate entries, we only update the parameters w.r.t. the query for efficiency. For instance, we only tune the branch w.r.t. the input modality for a two-branch VLM like CLIP. For image captioning, we construct the TTA pipeline with two methods (Mokady et al., 2021; Nukrai et al., 2022) built upon large language models (LLMs). During TTA, we only tune the projector which projects the image into the LLM token embedding space. Plus, several task-agnostic practical tricks are applied, i.e., multiple reward models, episodic TTA, and momentum buffer for incremental learning. To summarize our contributions: 1) To the best of our knowledge, RLCF is the first universal fully TTA framework for improving the zero-shot generalization capacity of VLMs across different tasks. 2) We develop a novel reward function for test time RL with CLIP. It is simple yet effective. Compared to previous methods in the training stage, it demonstrates that CLIP can be used as a practical reward model alone, even with a single test sample. 3) We design task-specific TTA pipelines for three VL tasks with RLCF. Extensive experiments with promising results validate the effectiveness of RLCF in boosting the zero-shot performance of different VLMs. RELATED WORK Reinforcement learning in language and vision The most well-known application of RL in natural language process is reinforcement learning with human feedback (RLHF) (Ouyang et al., 2022; OpenAI, 2023). A reward model is trained with preference data collected from humans, and it is used to fine-tune the LLM via proximal policy optimization (PPO, ). Similar approaches are applied in (Ziegler et al., 2019; Stiennon et al., 2020; Bai et al., 2022; Glaese et al., 2022). In prompt engineering for language models, RLPrompt and TEM- PERA search for discrete text prompts by RL. RL has also been widely applied in vision and multi-modal research. A comprehensive study of deep RL in computer vision can be found at. Recently, Pinto et al. optimize vision task metrics using RL and achieve promising results, demonstrating the effectiveness of RL in vision. In the multi-modal area, ImageReward collects preference data and trains a reward model for text-to-image generation tasks, similar to RLHF in GPT models. SCST apply CIDEr metric as a reward function with REINFORCE algorithm to improve the generation quality in image captioning during training. Cho et al. explore the possibility of using CLIPScore as the reward in image captioning. Their empirical results show that CLIPScore cannot be an independent reward function and should be combined with a grammar regularization or CIDEr metric. Nevertheless, the training of the grammar head and calculation of CIDEr metric both need reference text, which is unavailable at test time. Test-time adaptation Test-time adaptation (TTA) aims to address the distribution shift between training and test data during test time (Sun et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2021a). Testtime training (TTT, ) allows modifications to the training pipeline. In such cases, self-supervised auxiliary tasks are incorporated to help the model adapt to the distribution of test data (Sun et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2023). For example, TTT+ utilizes instance discrimination tasks from contrastive learning. On the other hand, fully TTA assumes that the training pipeline cannot be modified as the training data is unavailable. Two popular techniques in fully TTA are normalization layer adaptation and entropy minimization. Normalization layer adaptation updates data statistics or parameters of the normalization layer based on batched test samples (Wang et al., 2021a; Schneider et al., 2020; Niu et al., 2023) or augmented data views from a single test sample. Entropy minimization aims to make the model confident in its predictions to reduce generalization error (Wang et al., 2021a; Zhang et al., 2022a; Manli et al., 2022; Niu et al., 2022; 2023). There is also a retrieval-augmented TTA method, which uses CLIP to retrieve informative data from an external large dataset and update the decision boundary during test time. METHOD 3.1 PRELIMINARIES Fully test-time adaptation in vision-language tasks Let fθ(·) represent a VLM trained on imagetext pairs Dtrain = {(ti, vi)}N i=1 with parameter θ, where ti ∈ Ttrain (training text space) and vi ∈ Vtrain (training image space). The objective of TTA (Sun et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021a) is to boost fθ(t) or fθ(v) on domain-shifted test samples Dtest = {(tj}M j=1 or Dtest = {(vj}M j=1, where tj ∈ Ttest (testing text space), vj ∈ Vtest (testing image space), Ttest ̸= Ttrain, and Vtest ̸= Vtrain. We assume that the VLM takes either text or image as input and outputs the other modality. In fully TTA, the training data are unavailable, and the training pipeline cannot be modified. Following TPT and MEMO, the adaptation is conducted with a single test point, i.e., the VLM is exposed to only one tj or vj. Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) CLIP comprises an image encoder g(·) and a text encoder h(·). CLIP is pre-trained using a contrastive loss that encourages similarity between feature vectors of paired images and text, aligning them in a shared embedding space. Once pre-trained, CLIP can assess the similarity between the text t and image v as follows: CLIP(t, v) = cos(h(t), g(v)), (1) where cos(·, ·) represents the cosine similarity. For image classification with CLIP, the input text consists of the prompt plus the class names, i.e., t = {pt; "dog"}, where prompt pt = "a photo of a". 3.2 TEST-TIME ADAPTATION WITH CLIP REWARD 3.2.1 REINFORCEMENT LEARNING WITH CLIP FEEDBACK Without loss of generality, we first consider the case where the VLM fθ(·) takes an image v as input and maps it to text t. During TTA, our goal is to learn a conditional distribution P(t|v, θ) = fθ(v) that maximizes a reward function R(·, ·). Formally, the optimization problem during TTA is: max θ Et∼P (·|v,θ)R(t, v). (2) Different from previous methods (Rennie et al., 2017; Cho et al., 2022; Pinto et al., 2023) which maximizes the expected reward over batched training samples, here we only maximize the expected reward over a single test sample v ∈ Vtest. Policy gradient with REINFORCE To compute the gradient of the non-differentiable reward function, REINFORCE is adopted to calculate ∇θEt∼P [R(t, v)]. It uses the so-called "log-derivative trick" to estimate the gradient of the expected reward for a given input: ∇θEt∼P [R(t, v)] = Et∼P [R(t, v)∇θ log P(t|v; θ)]. (3) In a VL task, the input and output modalities are closely related, e.g., the input is an image and the output is the description of the image. Therefore, we can use CLIP to evaluate the similarity between the input and output, and the model can maximize this similarity to align with task goals. Similar to, we use CLIPScore as the reward: CLIP-S(t, v) = w × max(CLIP(t, v), 0), (4) where w = 2.5 is a constant. CLIPScore is always non-negative, which means it encourages all model behaviors. However, for an irrelevant sampled image-text pair in Figure 1b, we expect the reward model to provide negative feedback to discourage such behavior. Cho et al. adopt a greedy search baseline which needs to be combined with a grammar regularization or CIDEr metric to be a practical reward function. In this work, we demonstrate that with proper sampling strategies and baseline, CLIPScore can also be used as the sole reward function in different VL tasks. Specifically, we set the reward baseline as the average CLIPScore of sampled image-text pairs. The reward function with baseline becomes: R(t, v) = CLIP-S(t, v) − Et∼P [CLIP-S(t, v)]. (5) It is straightforward to get the reward function for a VLM which takes text t as input and return an image v according to Eq. (5). The sampling strategies will be presented in the next section. 3.2.2 TASK-SPECIFIC FULLY TEST-TIME ADAPTATION RLCF is flexible and applicable across various VL tasks, and we apply RLCF to three different VL tasks in this work. For all tasks, the VLM solely learns through REINFORCE with Eq. (5) as the reward function during test time. However, VLMs and sampling strategies vary with tasks. One point that needs to be clarified is why using the CLIP reward as feedback rather than directly fine-tuning the model with CLIP supervision. For example, methods like knowledge distillation (KD, ) or pseudo-label. InstructGPT demonstrates that model learning with feedback has better generalization capabilities compared to a supervised fine-tuning model. In our context, KD or pseudo-label requires a weak model (student) to mimic a strong model (teacher). However, it is worth noting that the student may be correct while the teacher may be incorrect. For instance, given an image of a dog, the top-3 predictions of the student and teacher models are {dog, horse, tree} and {cat, dog, horse}, respectively. For KD or pseudo-label, the student will be forced to follow the incorrect behaviors of the teacher. In contrast, the feedback mechanism only assesses the sampled results from the student, less likely to alter the correct prediction. In such cases, the feedback mechanism combines the merits of both the student and the teacher. Another important reason is that CLIP supervision cannot be directly used in generalization tasks like image captioning, while the feedback mechanism is universal. Multiple reward models with weights By default, a single CLIP-ViT-L/14 is used as the reward model. An ensemble of multiple reward models can be used for better feedback. We assign scores based on human preference for different CLIP models: {CLIP-ViT-L/14-336: 10, CLIP-ViT-L/14: 5, CLIP-RN50×64: 3}. These scores are then normalized to sum up to 1, serving as weights for the ensemble. CLIP-RN uses a ResNet as the image encoder, while CLIP-ViT adopts a vison transformer. Episodic TTA The model is exposed to only a single test sample once, making the learned knowledge unreliable for other samples. Hence, after each TTA process, the model parameters θ are reset to the initial state θ⋆ like (Wang et al., 2021a; Manli et al., 2022). It is called episodic TTA. Momentum buffer While episodic TTA ensures reliability, it limits the incremental learning ability of the model. To address this issue, we introduce a momentum buffer ξ, initialized as ξ ← θ⋆. After a TTA process, θ becomes θ, and ξ is updated by ξ ← mξ + (1 − m)θ, where m ∈ [0, 1) is a momemtum coefficient. Every Bs samples, we update θ⋆ ← ξ. At the start of the next TTA process, θ ← θ⋆, allowing the utilization of the learned knowledge. The momentum buffer functions similarly to an ensemble of different models, resembling model soups. CONCLUSION In this work, we introduce reinforcement learning with CLIP feedback (RLCF) to improve the zeroshot generalization ability of VLMs on the fly. A novel reward function with CLIP is developed. We instantiate three TTA pipelines for image classification, text-image retrieval, and image captioning with task-specific sampling strategies and parameter tuning manners. With RLCF, the zero-shot generalization capacity of various VLMs is boosted significantly. We hope RLCF can provide heuristic information for future research that employs TTA with feedback from large foundation models.

papers.title: Tackling the Zero-Shot Reinforcement Learning Loss Directly
papers.abstract: Zero-shot reinforcement learning (RL) methods aim at instantly producing a behavior for an RL task in a given environment, from a description of the reward function. These methods are usually tested by evaluating their average performance on a series of downstream tasks. Yet they cannot be trained directly for that objective, unless the distribution of downstream tasks is known. Existing approaches either use other learning criteria [BBQ+ 18, TRO23, TO21, HDB+ 19], or explicitly set a prior on downstream tasks, such as reward functions given by a random neural network [FPAL24]. Here we prove that the zero-shot RL loss can be optimized directly, for a range of non-informative priors such as white noise rewards, temporally smooth rewards, ``scattered'' sparse rewards, or a combination of those. Thus, it is possible to learn the optimal zero-shot features algorithmically, for a wide mixture of priors. Surprisingly, the white noise prior leads to an objective almost identical to the one in VISR [HDB+19], via a different approach. This shows that some seemingly arbitrary choices in VISR, such as Von Mises--Fisher distributions, do maximize downstream performance. This also suggests more efficient ways to tackle the VISR objective. Finally, we discuss some consequences and limitations of the zero-shot RL objective, such as its tendency to produce narrow optimal features if only using Gaussian dense reward priors.
