Hereafter, we will operate in the regime of Deep Reinforcement Learning (Arulkumaran et al., 2017; Li, 2017), where value functions, policies or dynamics models are, unless otherwise stated, approximated with deep neural networks (Goodfellow et al., 2016; LeCun et al., 2015). Deep RL is the most recent incarnation of works that use function approximation in RL, typically to deal with large or continuous state and action spaces (Baird, 1995; Precup et al., 2001; Sutton et al., 1999a). We will often discuss the loss function L against which a model is optimised. We do not discuss this optimisation process in detail; in practice this involves optimisation algorithms like Adaptive Moment Estimation (ADAM) and Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) (Bottou, 1998; Robbins and Monro, 1951) updating model parameters in proportion to gradients obtained by backpropogation. 2.1.4 Model-free Reinforcement Learning RL methods that search for the optimal policy without explicitly modelling the environment’s dynamics are said to be model-free. They expedite this search either by approximating the optimal policy directly, learning the optimal value function (and deriving the policy indirectly via Equation 2.1), or a combination of both. In this section we will introduce the preferred methods in these three classes. Policy gradient methods. Methods that estimate the optimal policy directly from experience rely on the policy gradient theorem. For a policy πθ(a|s) parameterised by θ, the policy gradient theorem says that the gradient of the expected return with respect to the parameters is given by ∇θJ(θ) = Eπθ [∇θ log πθ(at|st) Gt], (2.8) where Gt = �T−t k=0 γkrt+k is the discounted return from timestep t to the terminal timestep T. Provided a state-action-return triple (st, at, Gt), the parameters of the policy are updated via θ ← θ + α · ∇θJ(θ), (2.9) where α ∈ R is a learning rate. The canonical policy gradient algorithm, REINFORCE, estimates Gt with Monte Carlo rollouts of a fixed policy in the environment; more recent methods like Trust Region Policy Optimisation (TRPO) and Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) instead use surrogate objectives involving value functions to stabilise learning. An advantage of policy gradient methods is their ability to handle large or continuous action spaces, which is required for many real-world problems. The cost of this is high data inefficiency. Value-Based Methods. Q-learning is the canonical value-based method (Dayan and Watkins, 1992; Watkins, 1989). The key idea is that the agent maintains a running estimate ˆQ(s, a) of the optimal action-value function Q∗(s, a). Given a transition (s, a, r, s′), ˆQ is updated via ˆQ(s, a) ← ˆQ(s, a) + α · δ, (2.10) where δ = r + γ maxa′∈A ˆQ(s′, a′) − ˆQ(s, a) is the temporal difference error in the estimate of ˆQ(s, a), and α ∈ R is a learning rate. Updating value functions in proportion to their temporal difference error, or TD learning (Samuel, 1959; Sutton, 1984, 1988), is central to nearly all modern RL algorithms that utilise value functions. A seminal moment in the field came when combined Q- learning with deep neural networks to produce Deep Q-Networks (DQN). Now, the running estimate ˆQ(s, a) of the optimal value function is approximated by a neural network Qϕ(s, a) with parameters ϕ and Equation 2.10 is converted to a mean squared error loss L on ϕ: LDQN(ϕ) = E(s,a,r,s′)∼D �� Qϕ(s, a) − (r + γ max a′∈A Qϕ−(s′, a′)) �2�, (2.11) where D is a replay buffer that stores previously observed transitions, and ϕ− are parameters of a target network updated periodically to improve stability. DQN was the first RL method to exhibit superhuman performance on the Arcade Learning Environment, and so catalysed the field of Deep RL. Many works have since built atop the framework of Deep Q-learning (Dabney et al., 2018; Gu et al., 2016; Hessel et al., 2018; Hester et al., 2018; Van Hasselt et al., 2016). Conveniently, methods that learn value functions can arrive at the optimal policy using an order of magnitude less data than methods that attempt to extract the optimal policy directly. There is not a single explanation for this, but a useful characteristic of Q learning methods are there ability to learn from off-policy data, that is, data derived from a policy different from the our current policy or the optimal policy. This is a core idea in Offline Reinforcement Learning, a key field in this thesis, which we explore in depth in §2.2. The primary drawback of value-based methods is the need to maintain an accurate value function for all (s, a) ∈ S × A which usually limits their applicability to problems with small, discrete action spaces. Value-based methods address the data inefficiency of policy gradient methods by using off-policy data to learn value functions. This comes at the cost of only being able to maintain predictions for a small, discrete set of actions. Ideally, we’d like to combine the data-efficiency of value-based methods, with the action-space flexibility of policy-gradient methods. The next section discusses this combination Actor critic methods. Actor Critic methods attempt to leverage the best aspects of policy gradient and value-based approaches (Grondman et al., 2012; Konda and Tsitsiklis, 1999; Peters and Schaal, 2008). The usual setup involves an actor, which is a policy πθ(a|s) with parameters θ as in policy gradient methods, and a critic, which is a value function Qϕ(s, a) with parameters ϕ as in DQN. The actor is updated to maximise the values predicted by Qϕ(s, a). Past works fall in two categories: those with stochastic policies, and those with deterministic policies. The canonical method in the first category is Soft Actor Critic (SAC); and the canonical method in the second category is Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and its derivatives Twin Delayed Deep Deterministic policy gradient (TD3) and TD7. No method has proven to consistently outperform the others. In this thesis the line of work that is continued in §3 and §4 leverages the deterministic policy actor-critic framework, specifically TD3. As a result, we introduce they key ideas behind TD3 below. TD3 addresses two failings of previous actor-critic methods. The first is the tendency for Q values to be overestimated because of the max operator inside the TD error of Equation 2.10, which is further exacerbated by function approximation. The second is the tendency for deterministic policies to overfit to peaks in the value function and so not explore the action-space efficiently. TD3 addresses the first failing with a clipped variant of Double Q-learning, where two critics Qϕ1 and Qϕ2 are updated towards the minimum of their predictions. TD3 addresses the second failing by adding Gaussian noise to actions used in the critic update which has the effect of assigning similar value to nearby actions in the state-action space. As a result, the loss function for critic i with parameters ϕi is a subtle evolution of the DQN loss (Equation 2.11) LTD3(ϕi) = E(s,a,r,s′)∼D �� Qϕi(s, a) − (r + γ min i=1,2 Qϕ− i (s′, (πθ(s′) + ϵ)) �2�, (2.12) where ϵ ∼ clip(N(0, σ), −c, c) is 0-mean Gaussian noise with variance σ, clipped in [−c, c]. The policy loss is derived from the predictions from the first critic Qϕ1 LTD3(θ) = −Es∼D [Qϕ1(s, πθ(s))]. (2.13) 2.1.5 One-step Model-based Reinforcement Learning A key characteristic of the RL problem (§2.1) is that the system dynamics are unknown to the agent a priori. The methods discussed in §2.1.4 deal with this by implicitly encoding the dynamics in the value function or policy. But is there benefit to modelling the system dynamics explicitly? That is the question asked in Model-based Reinforcement Learning (MBRL) (Moerland et al., 2023; Polydoros and Nalpantidis, 2017). Research on MBRL was catalysed by the Dyna algorithm which built the framework that most modern MBRL algorithms follow. Here, the model is some function fθ with parameters θ that approximates the one- step system dynamics and (optionally) the one-step reward, that is, it directly approximates P(st+1|st, at) and (optionally) R(st+1)3. The model is used to generate synthetic experience for updating the policy in a process called planning. The benefit of planning is that it is conducted without interacting with the environment, which can greatly reduce the amount of real experience required to learn a policy. The remainder of this section will discuss popular modelling and planning methods. Dynamics models. The most data-efficient MBRL method to-date is PILCO which models the system dynamics using Gaussian Processes (Engel et al., 2005; Kuss and Rasmussen, 2003; Williams and Rasmussen, 2006), and solves the cartpole swing-up task with 20 seconds of experience. This spurred others to experiment with Gaussian Processes for MBRL (Deisenroth et al., 2013; Grande et al., 2014; Kamthe and Deisenroth, 2018; Levine et al., 2011; Sæmundsson et al., 2018), but unfortunately inference using a dataset of size n has complexity O(n3) which becomes unwieldy with more than a few thousand samples. Deep neural networks scale more favourably and have been used as a substitute (Clavera et al., 2018; Lambert et al., 2019; Nagabandi et al., 2018c). The most straightforward approach uses a model fθ to predict the state st+1 that follows (st, at) via maximum likelihood estimation (MLE). Given a dataset of transitions D = {(st, at, st+1)i}|D| i=1, the standard MLE loss is Lmodel(θ) = −E(st,at,st+1)∼D [log fθ(st+1|st, at)]. (2.14) Unlike Gaussian Processes, a network trained with the standard MLE loss does not quantify uncertainty in its predictions. More recent works like Probabilistic Ensembles with Trajectory Sampling (PETS) address this by training an ensemble of neural networks to predict a multivariate Gaussian distribution over the next state i.e. fθ(N(µθ(st+1), σθ(st+1)) | st, at). Each member of the ensemble has a different weight initialisation and is trained on a different subset of D (Clavera et al., 2018; Janner et al., 2019; Lakshminarayanan et al., 2017), meaning their aggregated predictions provide some estimate of epistemic uncertainty, and the multivariate Gaussian provides some estimate of aleatoric uncertainty. PETS reduced the amount of data required to complete 3A common assumption is that the ground truth reward function is available for calculating the rewards associated with model predictions. In this case learning an approximation of the reward function is unnecessary. standard MuJoCo benchmark tasks by more than 10x over state-of-the-art model-free methods like PPO. World models. The methods discussed above operate on sensor-based states (e.g. joint torques and velocities), but in many real cases it is more convenient to operate on pixel-based states derived from cameras. If we were to naively apply the models discussed thus far on pixel-based states they would be required to predict the change in pixel intensity for all pixels in the image, which becomes impractical for any realistic image resolution. Instead, it is common to encode the image-based state into a compact, low-dimensional latent space, then train a model to predict the latent dynamics in this low- dimensional space (Banijamali et al., 2018; Hafner et al., 2019b; Watter et al., 2015). Methods following this routine are often called world models (Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018; Schmidhuber, 1990a,b, 2015), with the preeminent work being the Dreamer family. The simplest setup involves a representation network pθ(zt|zt−1, at−1, ot) that predicts latent state z given the previous latent state, action, and image observation ot, and a latent dynamics model qθ(zt|zt−1, at−1) that predicts the next latent state given the current latent state and action. The representation network is a convolutional neural network and the latent dynamics model is a recurrent neural network (Chung et al., 2014; Hafner et al., 2019b). DreamerV2 was the first method to exhibit superhuman performance on the Arcade Learning Environment by training a policy using data generated solely by a latent dynamics model. If the world model cannot be paired with a ground-truth reward function, then an approximate reward model must be learned from data. This can be achieved with reward-labelled states, via human feedback, via an observer’s preference for one trajectory over another (Ibarz et al., 2018; Sadigh et al., 2017), or using inverse RL. Planning. How is a model of the system dynamics and rewards used to select the right action? The canonical planning algorithm is Model Predictive Control (MPC) (Allgöwer and Zheng, 2012; Borrelli et al., 2017; Camacho and Alba, 2013; Garcia et al., 1989; Morari and Lee, 1999). Provided a dynamics model fθ, reward function R, and initial state st, MPC searches for the sequence of actions A∗ H = (at,..., at+H−1) that maximise reward over horizon H A∗ H = arg max A∗ H H−1 � k=0 Efθ [R(st+k) | st+k+1 = fθ(sk, ak)]. (2.15) Approximate solutions tend to be used in lieu of an analytical solution. These include random-shooting, which involves populating a matrix of random action sequences, rolling them out to horizon H, and executing the first action from the sequence with highest predicted reward. The Cross Entropy Method (CEM), and Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) follow a similar routine, but perform several iterations of action selection matrix population, where each new iteration skews the samples towards action sequences with higher predicted reward. A second popular planning algorithm is Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS), as used by game-playing algorithms like AlphaGo, AlphaGo Zero, AlphaZero and MuZero. MCTS creates a search tree where the nodes are states and edges are actions sampled from a policy network. The tree of predicted future states is populated according to dynamics fθ and rewards are calculated according to Rϕ. The reward statistics are aggregated across the tree and an action is sampled from a distribution weighted with respect to expected future reward. This procedure has been shown to be remarkably effective when the action-space is discrete, as is the case in the games mastered by the algorithms described above. However, in this thesis, and in most realworld problems, we are concerned exclusively with continuous action spaces where planning with MCTS is infeasible. Equipped with a world model that accurately simulates the environment dynamics, a reward model that specifies a task of interest, and a planning algorithm or policy for selecting actions that maximise the reward model §2.1.4, an agent can be trained entirely in simulation to generalise to one task in the real-world zero-shot (Rigter et al., 2023; Sekar et al., 2020). Problems arise, however, if we want the agent to solve multiple tasks zero-shot. This would require learning multiple reward models, then training multiple distinct policies in parallel. To what extent does that approach scale? In the following section we will discuss methods that attempt to bypass this problem, learning policies in simulation that can generalise to many tasks. 2.1.6 Multi-step Model-based Reinforcement Learning So far we have discussed different methods for summarising an MDP to inform policy selection. In §2.1.3 we discussed value functions which are methods for summarising the long-run utility of states, actions and policies. Value functions are far-sighted insofar as they model the reward an agent following some policy can expect to receive far into the future4. In §2.1.5 we discussed dynamics models which are methods for summarising the short-run evolution of the state when taking some action, from which its utility can be derived via a reward model. Dynamics models are near-sighted insofar as they model the reward an agent following some policy can expect to receive in the short-term (where “shortness” here is mediated by how accurate the model remains as the planning horizon is lengthened). In this section we shall discuss a third class of methods which we think of as far-sighted dynamics models. Informally, instead of answering the question of how likely the agent is to reach some next state, they answer how likely the agent is to reach some future state that may not be accessible for many timesteps. As we shall see, methods capable of providing such answers have useful, unique properties. There is no agreed-upon name for this class of methods in the literature so we call them multi-step model-based reinforcement learning methods. Successor representations. Work on multi-step model-based RL methods began with the successor representation (SR). For an MDP with discrete state and action spaces, the SR Mπ(s0, a0) of state-action pair (s0, a0) when following policy π is defined as the expected discounted sum of future occurrences of each state in the state space: M π(s0, a0, s):= Eπ,P � T � t=0 γt1(st+1 = s) | (s0, a0) � ∀ s ∈ S. (2.16) The SR can answer the following informal question: “how often am I likely to pass through state s when following policy π”. This formulation has a valuable characteristic: it can be used to derive the value function Qπ R for policy π with respect to reward function R using only linear operations Qπ R(s0, a0) = � s∈S M π(s0, a0, s)R(s). (2.17) Successor features and successor measures. SRs operate on MDPs with discrete state and action spaces. Recent work has generalised the core ideas to MDPs with continuous state and action spaces, with this first to do so being Barreto et al.’s successor features (SFs). The SFs ψπ of 4Indeed, in the case of non-episodic MDPs, value functions summarise expected reward over infinite time-horizons, with the degree to which the future is considered mediated by the discount factor γ. state-action pair (s0, a0) are defined as the expected discounted sum of future state features subject to the system dynamics and policy: ψπ(s0, a0):= Eπ,P � T � t=0 γtφ(st+1) | (s0, a0) �, (2.18) where φ: S → Rd is a feature-map that embeds states in a d-dimensional space. Note that if the state space is discrete, and if the features are a onehot encoding of the state into R|S|, then we recover the definition of the SR (Equation 2.16). Instead of the reward being a function of the state, it is then assumed that reward is a linear function of the features i.e. R(s) = φ(s)⊤w where w ∈ Rd are the reward weights. As a result, like with SRs in Equation 2.17, the value function for policy π and reward R can be quickly recovered from the successor features: Qπ R(s0, a0) = Eπ,P � T � t=0 γtR(st+1) � = Eπ,P � T � t=0 γtφ(st+1)⊤ � wR = ψπ(s0, a0)⊤wR. (2.19) An alternative approach is based on successor measures. Here, instead of computing the discounted sum of future features, it is the discounted probability of reaching some subset of the state space in the future that is computed: M π(s0, a0, X):= T � t=0 γtPrπ,P(st+1 ∈ X | s0, a0) ∀ X ⊂ S, (2.20) where Prπ,P(·|s0, a0) is the probability of some event occurring subject to policy π, dynamics P and initial state-action pair (s0, a0). Both SFs and SMs are closely related to Sutton et al.’s general value functions which view the reward expectation computed by traditional value functions (Equations 2.3 and 2.4) as a special case of a more general cumulant, that is, any property of an MDP’s long-term behaviour that may be of interest for finding the optimal policy. In the case of SFs the cumulants are the state features, and in the case of SMs the cumulant is the state visitation probability. Universal successor representations. SRs, SFs, and SMs are all defined with respect to some policy π. In this section we shall introduce the final, most general multi-step model-based RL methods which disentangle the policy from SFs and SMs. In the case of SFs this is achieved with universal successor features; and in the case of SMs this is achieved with forward-backward representations. The unifying idea between these methods is to condition the long-run dynamics predictions on some parameterisation of the policy to allow the expected behaviour of different policies to be compared. This idea is similar to Schaul et al.’s universal value function approximators which condition the value function on a goal state. We shall discuss each method in turn. Consider a set of policies πz parameterised by z ∈ Rd. Universal successor features (USFs) ψ: S × A × Rd → Rd, compute the expected future features of some state-action pair conditioned on the policy induced by z ψ(s0, a0, z) = Eπz,P � T � t=0 γtφ(st+1) | s0, a0 � ∀ (s0, a0) ∈ S × A, z ∈ Rd. (2.21) The policy is trained to maximise the value function induced by setting wR = z πz(s):= arg max a ψ(s, a, z)⊤z ∀ (s, a) ∈ S × A, z ∈ Rd. (2.22) If Equation 2.22 holds, then the policy πz is approximately optimal for the task defined by reward weights wR = z. Forward-backward representations apply a similar idea in the context of successor measures. Here, a forward model F: S × A × Rd → Rd and a backward model B: S → Rd are trained to jointly approximate the successor measure: M πz(s0, a0, X) ≈ � X F(s0, a0, z)⊤B(s, a)ρ(ds) ∀ (s0, a0) ∈ S×A, X ⊂ S, z ∈ Rd, (2.23) where ρ is the distribution of states viewed by the agent. The forward embedding of state-action pair (s0, a0) can be thought of as summarising their expected future trajectories subject to a policy parameterised by z. Because this summarisation is compressed into representation space Rd, this is functionally identical to a USF with feature embedding space Rd. The backward embedding B of a state s+ can be thought of as summarising the possible routes to s+. If the dot product of these two embeddings F ⊤B is large, then s+ is reachable from (s0, a0). With the forward model being functionally equivalent to universal successor features, the policy is trained identically πz(s):= arg max a F(s, a, z)⊤z ∀ (s, a) ∈ S × A, z ∈ Rd. (2.24) * * * We began this chapter with an introduction of the traditional reinforcement learning setting: an agent interacting with an environment to learn intelligent behaviour tabula rasa, with no prior knowledge. Another name for this setting is online reinforcement learning. The label online reflects the fact that, in some sense, the agent is always on the clock, interleaving new experiences, learning, planning and goal accomplishment. This framing deliberately mirrors a human life, a continuum of experience in which we too must interleave learning, planning and survival. However, can we provide them with some prior knowledge that might make online learning more sample efficient? This is the concern of offline reinforcement learning, the subject of the next section. 2.2 Offline Reinforcement Learning Offline reinforcement learning aims to build agents that solve tasks in environments without needing to interact with them (Ernst et al., 2005; Lange et al., 2012; Levine et al., 2020; Riedmiller, 2005). To achieve this the agent is provided a historical dataset of experience, collected by some other agent or controller, from which it must derive its own policy. The dataset is said to be offline because it is made available to the agent prior to online evaluation in the environment. There are practical motivations for this sort of pre-training. For most real-world problems the unconstrained trial-and-error learning implied by the online reinforcement learning setting is infeasible, costly or dangerous. Such problems are found in domains like healthcare, where trial-and-error learning could risk the patient’s health; industrial control, where trial-and-error learning could damage expensive infrastructure; or autonomous driving, where trial-and-error learning could endanger road users. As with the online setting, the environment is modelled as an MDP (§2.1.1), and the agent’s goal is to find a policy π that maximises the expected return (Equation 2.2). For training, the agent has access to a static dataset of Start Do✏ine Goal M Goal ⇡ Figure 2.2: Trajectory stitching in offline RL. (Left) A graph MDP M where the task is to find the shortest path to the goal state. (Middle) A dataset of offline trajectories Doffline that may not contain the optimal trajectory for the task. (Right) The policy π learns to combine sub-trajectories to find the shortest path to the goal. transitions Doffline = {(st, at, rt, st+1)}|Doffline| t=1 collected on its behalf by one or more unknown behaviour policies πβ. There are no specific assumptions made about πβ, but in general it is either a) optimal for the test task, or b) suboptimal for the test task. In the case of a), the offline RL problem collapses to an imitation learning problem where the agent only needs to copy the policy implicit in the dataset to maximise expected reward at test time. In the case of b), the agent must stitch together sub-optimal trajectories to find a policy that is different and better than that which created the dataset—Figure 2.2. It is case b) that interests the field because datasets demonstrating sub-optimal control are plentiful for most real-world problems. Only once the agent has used the dataset to learn a policy is it exposed to the environment for evaluation. Because the learned policy π must be different and better than the behaviour policy πβ, there will necessarily be a distribution shift between the states visited by π and πβ. This is true of the online setting too, but is less of a problem. There, the agent can find itself in parts of the state-space that it hasn’t yet observed, form “what-if” hypotheses about where actions may lead, then falsify them by executing the actions and observing the behaviour. Clearly, the offline setting doesn’t allow this luxury, so naïve application of online RL methods leads to irrecoverable prediction errors at states and actions not in Doffline (Kumar et al., 2019a; Levine et al., 2020). Past works have developed a set of methods for constraining the agent’s behaviour to be close to the training dataset, and so minimise the distribution shift. The degree to which the agent’s behaviour matches the dataset is the critical design decision for offline RL algorithms. At the left end lie methods that attempt to mimic πβ, the policy that produced the data. The further right one moves the less the methods attempt to mimic πβ and the closer they are to full RL methods. as a function of the deviation they allow—Figure 2.3. At one end sit methods that attempt to exactly copy the behaviour policy (also known as behaviour cloning ); at the other end sit methods that maximally deviate from the behaviour policy (which is equivalent to full reinforcement learning). The goal for any method is to move away from the behaviour policy to enable different and better behaviour, but not far enough to lose the grounding provided by the data. The following sections will cover the key works. We will begin with a review of policy constraints (§2.2.1), then value function constraints (§2.2.2), and finish with model constraints (§2.2.3). 2.2.1 Policy Constraints Policy constraint methods control how much the learned policy deviates from the behaviour policy. Batch-Constrained Deep Q-learning (BCQ) is the canonical policy-constraint offline RL method. Here, an approximation of the behaviour policy ˆπβ is made with a Conditional Variational Autoencoder, and actions are sampled from it when training a value function. To update the value function at state-action pairs not present in the dataset some of the actions are updated with a perturbation model ζ. The Q function is trained across a set of n perturbed actions {ai + ζ(s, ai, Φ)}n i=1 with ai ∼ ˆπβ, and Φ defining a range [−Φ, Φ] that constrains the perturbation. A nice property of BCQ is that the practitioner can control where π sits on the continuum in Figure 2.3 using Φ and n. Setting Φ = 0 and n = 1 dictates strict behaviour cloning of πβ. Increasing Φ and n encourages deviation from πβ, and as Φ, n → ∞ full reinforcement learning is recovered. Other works achieve a similar result without having to directly approximate πβ (Fakoor et al., 2021; Fujimoto et al., 2024; Ghasemipour et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2019b; Matsushima et al., 2020; Peng et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022, 2019; Yang et al., 2022b). Perhaps the most successful of these is TD3-BC, which adds a behaviour cloning term to the usual TD3 loss (Equation 2.12, §2.1.4): LTD3-BC(θ) = −E(s,a)∼Doffline � λQϕ(s, πθ(s)) − (πθ(s) − a)2�, (2.25) where λ controls the relative strength of the behaviour cloning term. This is related to work that uses importance sampling to align π and πβ (Gelada and Bellemare, 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Nachum et al., 2019; Precup et al., 2001; Sutton et al., 2016), but importance sampling has proven less successful empirically than methods akin to TD3-BC. A parallel research direction re-frames policy-constrained offline RL as a sequence-learning problem (Chebotar et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021; Furuta et al., 2021; Janner et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2022; Reed et al., 2022; Siebenborn et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Yamagata et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2022). The first to do so was the Decision Transformer (DT), whose key idea was to train the agent to imitate high-value trajectories contained in the dataset. The DT trajectory τ DT replaces the one-step reward in our definition of τ (§2.1.1) with the undiscounted return-to-go Gt = �T−t k=0 rt+k. Given a state space S ∈ RN and an action space A ∈ RM, each dimension forms an element of the trajectory of length H such that: τ DT = �..., s1 t, s2 t,..., sN t, a1 t, a2 t,..., aM t, Gt,... � t = 1,..., H. (2.26) A Transformer is trained to autoregressively predict the next token in the sequence as per the familiar language modelling setup;;. When the policy is rolled out at test-time, G0 is set to the maximum cumulative reward an agent could receive in the MDP. Subsequent return-to-gos are found by subtracting the observed one step reward from the previous return-to-go Gt = Gt−1 − rt. The hope is that by conditioning each action on an approximate maximum return, the Transformer will retrieve the action that maximised the return from that state in the dataset. 2.2.2 Value Function Constraints Value function constraint methods regularise the Q function at state-action pairs not present in the dataset. Recall, DQN’s value function loss from §2.1.4: LDQN(ϕ) = E(s,a,r,s′)∼D �� Qϕ(s, a) − (r + γ max a′∈A Qϕ−(s′, a′)) �2�. Note that the TD target (r + γ maxa′∈A Qϕ−(s′, a′)) contains a maximisation over the action space A. There is no guarantee that this action is present in the dataset which can lead to an overestimation of Q(s, a) ∀ (s, a) /∈ Doffline and a consequent biasing of the policy toward unseen actions. The canonical fix is Conservative Q-learning (CQL), which adds a new term to the DQN loss: LCQL(ϕ) = α · � Es∼Doffline[max a∈A Qϕ(s, a)] − E(s,a)∼Doffline [Qϕ(s, a)] � + LDQN, (2.27) where α is a scaling parameter. The CQL loss has the dual effect of minimising peaks in the current Q iterate, and maximising Q for state-actions pairs in the dataset. CQL learns a pessimistic estimate of the true value function, but more recent works have shown it to be more pessimistic than necessary (Garg et al., 2023; Lyu et al., 2022; Nair et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2022a). IQL allows the practitioner to “tune” how pessimistically the agent views out-of-distribution states and actions. IQL’s Q function loss is LIQL(θ) = E(s,a,r,s′)∼Doffline � (r + γVϕ(s′) − Qθ(s, a))2�, (2.28) where the state value function Vϕ is learned with LIQL(ϕ) = E(s,a)∼Doffline [Le 2 (Qθ−(s, a) − Vϕ(s))], (2.29) where Le 2(u) = (e − I(u < 0))u2) is the asymmetric least squares loss (also called expectile regression) on u, mediated by e ∈ [0, 1] with I representing the indicator function. Setting e = 0.5 returns the the expected value of the distribution, e ≥ 0.5 decreases pessimism and e < 0.5 increases pessimism. Value-constraint methods like CQL and IQL have consistently outperformed policy-constraint methods on the standard offline RL benchmarks like D4RL. 2.2.3 Model Constraints Model constraint methods penalise the predictions of the learned dynamics model at state-action pairs not in the dataset. The canonical method is Model- based Offline Reinforcement Learning (MOReL), which learns a pessimistic ensemble of Gaussian dynamics models ˆfθ, and an amended reward function ˆR. The key idea is to detect unknown state-actions (i.e. those not present in Doffline) with a function U(s, a), then force rollouts that pass through them to transition to an absorbing state HALT with high negative reward. The pessimistic dynamics model is given by: ˆfθ(s′|s, a) =    δ(s′ = HALT) if U(s, a) = TRUE or s = HALT ˆfθ(s′|s, a) otherwise, (2.30) where δ(s′ = HALT) is the Dirac delta function which forces the transition to absorbing state HALT. The pessimistic reward function is given by: ˆR(s) =    −κ if s = HALT R(s) otherwise. (2.31) where −κ is an arbitrarily large negative reward. The dynamics model is an ensemble of K models {fθ1,..., fθK}. If the difference in the predictions made by models in the ensemble exceeds some threshold λ for some state-action pair (s, a), then (s, a) is classified as unknown i.e. U(s, a) = maxi,j ||fθi(s, a)−fθj(s, a)||2 ≥ λ. Several other works are built around this idea (Argenson and Dulac-Arnold, 2020; Matsushima et al., 2020; Rafailov et al., 2021; Yu et al., 2020). A different approach is to use an analogue to U(s, a) to identify state-actions for CQL-style value function regularisation (Rigter et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2021b), which is useful in continuous action spaces where CQL’s max operator is tricky to estimate. * * * We have now introduced the two central paradigms of reinforcement learning. In online RL, we provide the agent direct, online access to the environment in which we evaluate its performance. It uses this access to perform trialand-error learning in its search for the optimal policy. In offline RL, the agent only receives indirect, offline access to the environment via a static dataset of pre-collected transitions. It uses this dataset to stitch together sub-optimal trajectories and return a policy that is different and better than the one that produced the dataset. Though these settings disagree on how the agent should access the environment, they agree on an important part of the problem specification: both the system dynamics P and task R do not change between training and testing. Unlike the methods discussed so far, humans have ways of dealing with situations that don’t conform to this assumption. Early steps have been made to replicate this ability in RL agents, steps we shall explore together in the next section. 2.3 Zero-Shot Generalisation in Reinforcement The traditional RL problem assumes the training and testing environments are identical. In this section we will relax this assumption, and discuss situations where there is some change in the environment at test time that the agent must deal with. We consider changes to either the reward function R or transition function P. We shall explore works that try to design agents to deal with such changes within the first deployment episode. In other words, these works want their agents to generalise to the new scenarios with zero practice shots5, which is where the sub-field derives its name: zero-shot generalisation (Kirk et al., 2023; Palatucci et al., 2009; Socher et al., 2013). Solving most real-world problems requires zero-shot generalisation. As we discussed in §2.2, unconstrained trial-and-error learning in the real-world is infeasible, so some amount of pre-training is inevitable. However, it is equally infeasible to think we can prepare an agent for every possible scenario it will face downstream. As a result, there will necessarily be some gap between training and deployment contexts that the agent must 5It is this restriction that distinguishes zero-shot generalisation from the related fields of Transfer Learning (Lazaric, 2012; Taylor and Stone, 2009) and Meta Reinforcement Learning (Finn et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2016). Though typical Transfer and Meta Reinforcement Learning setups also assume some change in the environment between training and testing, they assume the agent is allowed multiple episodes in the test context to adjust to the change. bridge to successfully solve problems. In more practical terms, this gap arises from mismatches between the real-world and pre-training worlds built with simulators or historical datasets. When we pre-train agents in simulation, it is extremely difficult to configure them to perfectly match the real-world, which is the well-established sim-to-real problem. When we pre-train with historical datasets, it is equally difficult to know if the dynamics of the real-world have changed in the interim, or to guarantee the task we want the agent to solve hasn’t switched away from the one solved in the dataset. None of the methods discussed so far have mechanisms for handling these discrepancies, but many other works do, and it is those that will be the focus of this section. We shall discuss problem settings where only the reward function or the system dynamics change between training and testing contexts. When we vary only the reward function between training and testing we call this task generalisation. When we vary only the dynamics function between training and testing we call this dynamics generalisation. To illustrate the difference consider an RL agent controlling a smart thermostat to maintain temperature setpoint Tset. If the agent were trained with Tset = 22oC, then tested with Tset = 18oC it must perform task generalisation to accommodate the change in setpoint. In contrast, if the agent were trained in residential building A with Tset = 22oC, then tested in office building B with Tset = 22oC it must perform dynamics generalisation to accommodate the change in building physics. Methods that attempt either type of generalisation fall into two categories: 1) those that increase the similarity between the train and test contexts, and 2) those that handle differences between the train and test contexts. Approach 1) hopes that if Ctrain is large enough it will subsume Ctest, that is, the test context may appear as just another variation in the train context. Approach 2) anticipates differences between Ctrain and Ctest and creates solutions for handling them explicitly. We shall use these categories to frame the remaining discussion, starting first with methods for task generalisation in §2.3.1 followed by methods for dynamics generalisation in §2.3.2. 2.3.1 Task Generalisation Increasing the similarity between train and test contexts. These methods attempt to train the agent on as many tasks as possible in the hope that one may prove sufficiently similar to the test task. This is most easily operationalised in the goal-conditioned RL setting (Kaelbling, 1993; Schaul et al., 2015) where the agent must learn a policy π(s, g) that minimises the number of steps taken to navigate to a goal state g ∈ S. Rewards are 1 if s = g, and 0 otherwise. Given a dataset of reward-free trajectories D = {(s0, a0,..., aT−1, sT)i}|D| i=1, we can label them with rewards under the assumption that the terminal state sT was the intended goal state g, and then use them to update any actor-critic algorithm. This method is called hindsight experience replay (HER), and it has the effect of creating a training context of goal-reaching tasks corresponding to all terminal states in the dataset. The wider the distribution of terminal states, the more goal-reaching tasks the agent will be trained to solve. A more general formulation is to instead assume that the goal state is any other state in the dataset, rather than the terminal state in each trajectory. In this setup, one trains a universal value function approximator (§2.1.6) Q(s, a, g) or V (s, g) where the goals are states sampled from D according to some pre-specified distribution. Methods that train V (s, g) are also called action-free RL methods, which are particularly helpful for training agents from vidoes that lack action data (Baker et al., 2022; Ghosh et al., 2023; Schmeckpeper et al., 2020). The primary drawback of these methods is they provide no principled mechanism for improving performance on non-goal-reaching (i.e. dense reward) tasks. For that we look to methods that handle the difference between the train and test contexts. Handling the differences between train and test contexts. Skill discovery methods are one way of performing generalisation to new tasks specified by dense reward functions (Da Silva et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2017; Sohn et al., 2018). Here, agents learn a set of skills which are combined by a learned hierarchical controller (Barto and Mahadevan, 2003; McGovern and Barto, 2001; Silver and Ciosek, 2012; Stolle and Precup, 2002; Sutton et al., 1999b) to solve the test task. In supervised skill discovery, the agent is provided a set of training reward functions that correspond to human-legible skills, like walking, standing or running for robotic locomotion. In unsupervised skill discovery (Eysenbach et al., 2018; Gregor et al., 2016; Jaderberg et al., 2016; Machado et al., 2017), the agent uses intrinsic rewards (Barto, 2013; Chentanez et al., 2004; Singh et al., 2010) to learn a distinct and separable set of skills. In-context RL methods train sequence models over contexts of historical states, actions and rewards (Duan et al., 2016; Grigsby et al., 2023; Laskin et al., 2022; Lu et al., 2024). The key idea is to condition the policy on these contexts, which act as examples of how one might complete the task. The canonical method, RL2, conditions an RNN on a single trajectory that covers several episodes, which it uses as examples to improve its own policy. This idea has received enthusiastic recent support because language models have shown an impressive ability to perform in-context learning (Brown et al., 2020b; Dong et al., 2022). The primary limitation of skill discovery and in-context RL is that they usually require many episodes of experience to perform task generalisation, which violates the one-episode experience constraint of zero-shot generalisation. * * * Touati et al. showed that the multi-step model-based RL methods discussed in §2.1.6 can be trained to zero-shot generalise to both goal-reaching tasks and dense reward tasks, thus unifying the approaches discussed in this section. If Equation 2.32 holds, then the policy will be approximately optimal for all tasks in the linear span of z, with z permitting both goal-reaching and dense reward tasks. The breadth of training tasks can be increased by increasing the representation dimension d. At test time, a small number of reward-labelled states Dlabelled = {(s, Rtest(s))} is used to infer the test task vector ztest by linear regression: ztest = arg minz Es∼Dlabelled � (Rtest(s) − φ(s)⊤z)2�, which is then used to condition the policy. A similar protocol is used for inferring the task vector with FB representations. Touati et al. pre-train FB representations and USFs on large, diverse offline datasets of transitions collected by exploratory algorithms on the DeepMind Control Suite. Remarkably, they show that FB representations can return zero-shot policies for unseen tasks that are ≈ 80% as performant as state-of-the-art RL methods trained to convergence on the task. As a result, these methods have recently been called foundation policies (FPs). 2.3.2 Dynamics Generalisation Increasing the similarity between train and test contexts. The easiest way to increase the similarity in dynamics between the train and test contexts is with domain randomisation (DR) (Peng et al., 2018; Sadeghi and Levine, 2016; Tobin et al., 2017). Here, we assume access to a parameterised simulation of the downstream task. For example, a robotic arm with free parameters θ ∈ Θ defining the arm’s mass, length, friction coefficients etc. Each episode the agent is trained on a new simulator instance with θ ∼ Unif(Θ). This incentivises a policy that is robust to changes in the dynamics defined by Θ. Another option is to sample parameters from a distribution that is biased toward those that improve some downstream performance metric like robustness, sample efficiency, or reward. This approach is called unsupervised environment design (Dennis et al., 2020; Jiang et al., 2021a,b; Parker-Holder et al., 2022; Wang et al., 2019), and was used to train a humanoid hand entirely in simulation to solves Rubik’s cubes with unseen initial configurations. The primary drawback of these approaches is that they require access to a simulator that already closely approximates physical reality. For many real-world problems no simulator exists, and so such methods are unusable. A closely related idea is data augmentation. Here, instead of randomising the parameters of the simulation, it is a dataset of experience that is randomised6. Given a dataset of transitions D = {(s, a, r, s′)i}|D| i=1, the most general approach is to create an operator Λ that augments each transition: Λ: (s, a, r, s′) �→ (λ ⊙ s, a, r, λ ⊙ s′) (2.33) with λ ∼ Unif([λlow, λhigh]|S|). Other works have pro- posed different state-based augmentation operators (Ball et al., 2021; Raileanu et al., 2020), or proposed analogous augmentations for pixel-based observations (Hansen et al., 2021; Hansen and Wang, 2021; Yarats et al., 2021). The difficulty here comes in selecting distribution bounds λlow and λhigh. They must be large enough to create qualitatively different dynamics, but not too large so that these dynamics are no longer physically realisable. No works have yet established a general method for setting these bounds, with each using task-dependent heuristics. 6In practice, the dataset can itself be simulated, or collected from the test context as in Offline RL (§2.2) Another solution is to collect a large, diverse dataset of experience covering many contexts, and meta-learning a policy across it (Chen et al., 2018a; Duan et al., 2016; Finn et al., 2017; Nagabandi et al., 2018a,b). This is the approach taken by GATO, a single, monolithic policy capable of solving robotics tasks, playing Atari and being a conversational chatbot. GATO is a decision transformer (§2.2.1) trained across a dataset of billions of tokens from hundreds of environments. An interesting thesis of this line of work is that learnings from one environment can help an agent in a seemingly unrelated environment. Examples include pre-training on Wikipedia articles to improve performance on Atari, or pre-training on open-source code to improve common sense reasoning. Of course, the primary drawback of these approaches is the difficulty of curating datasets that are both large and high-quality. Handling the differences between train and test contexts. The typical way to manage differences in train and test dynamics is to condition the policy on some representation of the context during training, then infer the unseen context quickly during testing. A successful first-effort was Yu et al.’s UP-OSI. Here, a policy is conditioned on a context provided by an encoder network which is trained to infer the context from a history of transitions. As long as the context can be inferred from a history length that is shorter than the episode length, UP-OSI can adapt to unseen dynamics within the first deployment episode. Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) combines the same idea with domain randomisation to cover a broader range of robotics test contexts, including broken joints and legs. These methods infer the dynamics context once from a fixed set of transitions. Another approach is to continuously infer the dynamics context from the agent’s recent history with memory models (Bakker, 2001; Beck et al., 2020; Hernandez- Gardiol and Mahadevan, 2000; Meng et al., 2021; Ramani, 2019; Schmidhuber, 2019; Wierstra and Schmidhuber, 2007; Zhang et al., 2016). Provided a history of observation-action pairs τk:n = xk,..., xn, with x = ϵ(o, a) being some encoding of an observation-action pair, a memory model is some function f that outputs a new hidden state hn given a past hidden state hk−1 and trajectory τk:n: hn = f(τk:n, hk−1). (2.34) During training, k = n − L in general, where L is a hyperparameter called the context length. During inference, k = n because the asymptotic time complexity is O(1) which is helpful for fast data collection, or high-frequency motor control. Equipped with memory, and trained over a distribution of dynamics contexts, agents can generalise well to unseen dynamics functions in the single-task setting (Ni et al., 2021; Zhao et al., 2019). Another line of work use hard-coded adaption techniques that do not need to infer a representation of the context. Seo et al.’s TW-MCL learns an ensemble of one-step dynamics models where each model predicts the next state for a fixed dynamics context. At test-time, they select the dynamics model with lowest prediction error on the observed transitions and use it for MPC planning. A similar approach is employed by MOLe, but here they are continually updating their ensemble of dynamics models to produce aggregate predictions that are accurate for the test context. 2.3.3 Without Prior Data The final and most demanding setting we shall discuss is one where the agent must solve a real-world task without any prior data. Here, the agent must do something akin to traditional system identification (Åström and Eykhoff, 1971; Ljung, 1998) i.e. collect a small, but expressive dataset from which to quickly learn a model or policy. The most impressive work in this setting is PILCO (discussed in §2.1.5), which models the system dynamics using Gaussian Processes and updates its policy with analytical gradients. Remarkably, PILCO solved the cartpole swing-up task with 20 seconds of real-world experience. Other works include Kendall et al.’s modelfree system (§2.1.4) which learned lane-following (autonomous driving), with only 30 minutes of self-collected experience; Lazic et al.’s agent that reduced energy consumption in data-centres by ≈ 10% using three hours of agent-collected data; and a series of works that learn robotic walking policies with 20 minutes, 90 minutes, and 120 minutes of experience, by configuring their critics with layer normalisation, dropout, and high update-to-data ratios. These results push the limits of data-efficiency in modern RL. However, we believe they signal the relative simplicity of the tasks, rather than the broader utility of the methods. The cartpole swing-up task has small state and action spaces, and requires motor control that is straightforward relative to other robotics tasks. Lane-following requires only that the controller keeps the car straight, paired with gentle pressure on the accelerator, which is simpler than, say, navigating a complex intersection. And controlling data-centre cooling equipment requires only that the agent cool as little as possible whilst satisfying generous temperature bounds. Nonetheless, these findings beg the question: are there any other real-world settings where data is scarce, and where relatively straightforward control could prove beneficial? In Chapter 5, we argue that emission-efficient building control is one such domain, and propose new methods that tackle it without prior data. Chapter 3 From Low Quality Data We begin our search for methods that solve real-world problems zero-shot by addressing the data quality constraint (§1.3). In §2.1.6 we introduced FB representations, and USFs, and in §2.3.1 we discussed how these methods can be used to perform zero-shot RL, as defined in. We relayed the surprising empirical finding that these methods can return policies for arbitrary tasks, for which they received no reward supervision during training, that are ≈ 80% as performant as state-of-the-art single task RL methods trained solely on each task. Unfortunately, these results are predicated on access to a large heterogeneous dataset of transitions for pre-training. In theory, such datasets could be curated by highly-exploratory agents during an upfront data collection phase (Burda et al., 2018; Eysenbach et al., 2018; Jaderberg et al., 2016; Jin et al., 2020; Liu and Abbeel, 2021a; Pathak et al., 2017, 2019). However, in practice, deploying such agents in real systems can be time-consuming, costly or dangerous. To avoid these downsides, it would be convenient to skip the data collection phase and pre-train on historical datasets. Whilst these are common in the real world, they are usually produced by controllers that are not optimising for data heterogeneity (§2.2), making them smaller and less diverse than current zero-shot RL methods expect. Can we still perform zero-shot RL using these datasets? This is the primary question this Chapter seeks to answer, and one we address in four parts. First, we investigate the performance of existing methods when trained on such datasets, finding their performance suffers because of out-of-distribution state- action value overestimation, a well-observed phenomenon in single-task offline RL. In §3.2.1, we explore the failure mode of existing methods on such datasets. Then, in §3.2.2, we propose straightforward amendments to these methods that address the failure mode. Finally, in §3.2.3, we illustrate the usefulness of our proposals with a controlled example. We develop our methods within the FB framework because of its superior empirical performance, but our proposals are also compatible with USF. We push their derivation to Appendix C.2.3 for brevity. 3.2.1 Failure Mode of Existing Methods To investigate the failure mode of existing methods we examine the FB loss (Equation 3.6) more closely. The TD target includes an action produced by the current policy at+1 ∼ πz(st+1). Equation 3.4 shows this is the policy’s current best estimate of the Q-maximising action in state s for task z. For finite datasets, this maximisation does not constrain the policy to actions observed in the dataset, and so it can become biased towards out-of-distribution (OOD) actions thought to be of high value. In such instances F and B are updated towards targets for which the dataset provides no support. This distribution shift is a well-observed phenomenon in single-task offline RL (Kumar et al., 2019a, 2020; Levine et al., 2020), and is exacerbated by small, low-diversity datasets as we explore in Figure 3.2. 3.2.2 Mitigating the Distribution Shift In the single-task setting, the distribution shift is addressed by applying con- straints to either the policy, value function or model (§2.2). Here we re-purpose single-task value function and model regularisation for use in the zero-shot RL setting. To avoid further complicating zero-shot RL methods, we only consider regularisation techniques that do not introduce new parametric functions. We discuss the implications of this decision in §3.4. Conservative Q-learning (CQL) regularises the Q function by querying OOD state-action pairs and suppressing their value. This is achieved by adding new term to the usual Q loss function LCQL = α · Es∼D,a∼µ(a|s)[Q(s, a)] − E(s,a)∼D[Q(s, a)]−H(µ) + LQ, (3.10) where α is a scaling parameter, µ(a|s) is a policy distribution selected to find the maximum value of the current Q function iterate, H(µ) is the entropy of µ used for regularisation, and LQ is the normal TD loss on Q. Equation 3.10 has the dual effect of minimising the peaks in Q under µ whilst maximising Q for state-action pairs in the dataset. We can replicate a similar form of regularisation in the FB framework, substituting F(s, a, z)⊤z for Q in Equation 3.10 and adding the normal FB loss (Equation 3.6) LVC-FB = α · (Es∼D,a∼µ(a|s),z∼Z[F(s, a, z)⊤z]−E(s,a)∼D,z∼Z[F(s, a, z)⊤z] − H(µ)) + LFB. (3.11) The key difference between Equations 3.10 and 3.11 is that the former suppresses the value of OOD actions for one task, whereas the latter does so for all task vectors drawn from Z. We call models learnt with this loss value-conservative forward-backward representations (VC-FB). Because FB derives Q functions from successor measures (Equation 3.5), and because (by assumption) rewards are non-negative, suppressing the predicted measures for OOD actions provides an alternative route to suppressing their Q values. As we did with VC-FB, we can substitute FB’s successor measure approximation F(s, a, z)⊤B(s+) into Equation 3.10, which yields: LMC-FB = α · (Es∼D,a∼µ(a|s),z∼Z,s+∼D[F(s, a, z)⊤B(s+)] −E(s,a)∼D,z∼Z,s+∼D[F(s, a, z)⊤B(s+)] − H(µ)) + LFB. (3.12) Equation 3.12 has the effect of suppressing the expected visitation count to goal state s+ when taking an OOD action for all task vectors drawn from Z, which says, informally, if we don’t know where OOD actions take us in the MDP, we assume they have low probability of taking us to any future states for all tasks. This is analogous to works that regularise model predictions in the single-task offline RL setting (Kidambi et al., 2020; Rigter et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2021b). As such, we call this variant a measure-conservative forward-backward representation (MC-FB). Since it is not obvious a priori whether the VC-FB or MC-FB form of conservatism would be more effective in practice, we evaluate both in §3.3. Implementing these proposals requires two new model components: 1) a conservative penalty scaling factor α and 2) a way of obtaining policy distribution µ(a|s) that maximises the current value or measure iterate. For 2), the choice of maximum entropy regularisation following ’s CQL(H) allows µ to be approximated conveniently with a log-sum exponential across Q values derived from the current policy distribution and a uniform distribution. Episodes begin with a point-mass initialised in the upper left of the maze (⊚), and the agent is tasked with selecting x and y tilt directions such that the mass is moved towards one of two goal locations (⊛ and ⊛). The action space is two-dimensional and bounded in [−1, 1]. We seek answers to four questions: (Q1) Can our proposals from §3.2 improve FB performance on small and/or low-quality exploratory datasets? (Q3) Do we sacrifice performance on full datasets for performance on small and/or low-quality datasets? (Q4) If our pre-training dataset only covers behaviour related to one downstream task (i.e. the dataset distribution is narrow and not exploratory), can our proposals from §3.2 improve FB performance on that task? 3.3.1 Setup Domains. To understand, we inspect the regularising effect of both models more closely. VC-FB regularises OOD actions on F(s, a, z)⊤z, with s ∼ D, and z ∼ Z, whilst MC-FB regularises OOD actions on F(s, a, z)⊤B(s+), with (s, s+) ∼ D and z ∼ Z. Note the trailing z in VC-FB is replaced with B(s+) in MC-FB which ties its updates to D further. We hypothesised that as |D| reduces, B(s+) provides poorer task coverage than z ∼ Z, hence the comparable performance on full datasets and divergent performance on 100k datasets. To test this, we evaluate a third conservative variant called directed (D)VC- FB which replaces all z ∼ Z in VC-FB with B(s+) such that OOD actions are regularised on F(s, a, B(s+))⊤B(s+) with (s, s+) ∼ D. This ties conservative updates entirely to D, and according to our above hypothesis, DVC-FB should perform worse than VC-FB and MC-FB on the 100k ExORL datasets. The state-of-the-art methods instantiate these ideas as either universal successor features (USFs) or forward-backward (FB) representations (Touati and Ollivier, 2021; Touati et al., 2023), with recent work showing the latter can be used to perform a range of imitation learning techniques efficiently. A representation learning method is required to learn the features for USFs, with past works using inverse curiosity modules, diversity methods (Hansen et al., 2019; Liu and Abbeel, 2021b), Laplacian eigenfunctions, or contrastive learning. No works have yet explored the issues arising when training these methods on low quality offline datasets, and only one has investigated applying these ideas to real-world problems. Goal-conditioned RL methods train policies to reach any goal state from any other state, and so can be used to perform zero-shot RL in goal-reaching environments (Eysenbach et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2022; Park et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023b). However, they have no principled mechanism for conditioning policies on “dense” reward functions (as such tasks are not solved by simply reaching a particular state), and so are not full zero-shot RL methods. A concurrent line of work trains policies using sequence models conditioned on reward-labelled histories (Chebotar et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2021; Furuta et al., 2021; Janner et al., 2021; Lee et al., 2022; Reed et al., 2022; Siebenborn et al., 2022; Xu et al., 2022; Yamagata et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2022), but, unlike zero-shot RL methods, these works do not have a robust mechanism for generalising to different reward functions as test-time. Offline RL Offline RL algorithms require regularisation of policies, value functions, models, or a combination to manage the offline-to-online distribution shift. Past works regularise policies with explicit constraints (Fakoor et al., 2021; Fujimoto et al., 2024, 2019a; Ghasemipour et al., 2021; Kumar et al., 2019b; Peng et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2022, 2019; Yang et al., 2022b), via important sampling (Gelada and Bellemare, 2019; Liu et al., 2019; Nachum et al., 2019; Precup et al., 2001; Sutton et al., 2016), by leveraging uncertainty in predictions (Bai et al., 2022; Jin et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2021; Zanette et al., 2021), or by minimising OOD action queries (Chen et al., 2020b; Kostrikov 3.6 Conclusion et al., 2021; Wang et al., 2018), a form of imitation learning. Other works constrain value function approximation so OOD action values are not overestimated (Kumar et al., 2019a, 2020; Lyu et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2021a,b; Yang et al., 2022a). Offline model-based RL methods use the model to identify OOD states and penalise predicted rollouts passing through them (Argenson and Dulac-Arnold, 2020; Kidambi et al., 2020; Matsushima et al., 2020; Rafailov et al., 2021; Rigter et al., 2022; Yu et al., 2021b, 2020). All of these works have focused on regularising a finite number of policies; in contrast we extend this line of work to the zero-shot RL setting which is concerned with learning an infinite family of policies. 3.6 In this chapter, we explored training agents to perform zero-shot RL from low quality data. We established that the existing methods suffer in this regime because they overestimate the value of out-of-distribution state-action values, a well-observed phenomena in single-task offline RL. As a resolution, we proposed a family of conservative zero-shot RL algorithms that regularise value functions or dynamics predictions on out-of-distribution state-action pairs. In experiments across various domains, tasks and datasets, we showed our proposals outperform their non-conservative counterparts in aggregate and sometimes surpass our task-specific baseline despite lacking access to reward labels a priori. In addition to improving performance when trained on sub- optimal datasets, we showed that performance on large, diverse datasets does not suffer as a consequence of our design decisions. We believe the proposals in this Chapter take a step toward managing the first of our three thesis constraints (§1.3). Chapter 4 Under Partial Observability So far, we have shown that we can improve the performance of zero-shot RL methods when subjected to the data quality constraint (§1.3). The data quality constraint says that real-world datasets lack the size and heterogeneity of toy datasets. We showed that, when trained on such datasets, standard zero-shot RL methods fail in predictable ways; they overestimate the values of state- action pairs not present in the dataset which poisons the policy. By regularising value functions to make conservative evaluations in such scenarios we went some way to addressing the failure mode and improving performance. Implicit in §3, and all prior results, is an assumed access to Markov states that provide the agent all the information it requires to solve a task. Though this is a common assumption in RL, for many interesting problems, the Markov state is only partially observed via unreliable or incomplete observations. Observations can be unreliable because of sensor noise or issues with telemetry. Observations can be incomplete because of egocentricity, occlusions or because they do not communicate a change to the environment’s task or dynamics context. This is our observability constraint (§1.3). How do zero-shot RL methods fare when subjected to the observability constraint? That is the primary question this Chapter seeks to answer, and one we address in three parts. First, we expose the mechanisms that cause the performance of standard zero-shot RL methods to degrade under partial observability (§4.2.1). Second, we repurpose methods that handle partial observability in single-task RL for use in the zero-shot RL setting, that is, we add memory models to the BFM framework (§4.2.2, Figure 4.1). Third, we conduct experiments that test how well zero-shot RL methods augmented with memory models manage partially observed states (§4.3.2) and partially 4.1 Preliminaries ⧖ ⧖ ⧖ ot z Dense Dense Memory ot ot-L at at-L ⧖ Dense Dense Memory o+-L o+ a+-L a+ = Figure 4.1: Zero-shot RL methods with memory. Let st ∈ S denote the Markov state at time t. When action at ∈ A is executed, the state updates via the transition function st+1 ∼ P(·|st, at), and the agent receives a scalar reward rt+1 ∼ R(st+1) and observation ot+1 ∼ O(·|st+1, at). The observation provides only partial information about the underlying Markov state. The agent samples actions from its policy at ∼ π(·|τ L t ), where τ L t = (at−L, ot−L+1,..., at−1, ot) is a trajectory of the preceding L observations and actions. We use T L to denote the set of all possible trajectories of length L. The policy is optimal in P if it maximises the expected discounted future reward i.e. π∗ = arg maxπ E[� t≥0 γtR(st+1)|s0, a0, π], where E[·|s0, a0, π] denotes an expectation over state-action sequences (st, at)t≥0 starting at (s0, a0) with st ∼ P(·|st−1, at−1) and at ∼ π(·|τ L t ), and γ ∈ [0, 1] is a discount factor. 4.1 Preliminaries Problem setting (partially observable zero-shot RL) In the standard zero-shot RL problem setting, states are fully observed. For pre-training, the agent has access to a static offline dataset of reward-free transitions D = {(si, ai, si+1)}|D| i=1, generated by an unknown behaviour policy. At test time, a task Rtest is revealed by labelling a small number of states in D to create a new dataset Dlabelled = {(si, Rtest(si))}k i=1 where typically k ≤ 10, 000. The agent must return a policy for this task with no further planning or learning. In this Chapter, we consider the extended problem setting of partially observable zero-shot RL. Here, the agent has access to an offline pre-training dataset of reward-free length-L trajectories, D = {τ L i }|D| i=1, each of which is a sequence of partial observations and actions. As before, a task Rtest is revealed at test time, for which the agent must return a policy. The task is specified by a small dataset of reward-labelled observation-action trajectories, where the reward is assumed to be a function of the final Markov state in the trajectory, Dlabelled = {(τ L i, Rtest(sL i ))}k i=1. Behaviour foundation models We build upon the forward-backward (FB) BFM which predicts successor measures. The successor measure M π(s0, a0, ·) over S is the cumulative discounted time spent in each future state st+1 after starting in state s0, taking action a0, and following policy π thereafter. Let ρ be an arbitrary state distribution and Rd be an embedding space. FB representations are composed of a forward model F: S×A×Rd → Rd, a backward model B: S → Rd, and set of polices π(s, z)z∈Rd. In §4.2.1, we explore the ways in which standard zero-shot RL methods fail in this setting. Then, in §4.2.2, we propose new methods that address these failures. We develop our methods in the context of FB, but our proposals are fully compatible with USF-based zero-shot RL methods. We report their derivation in Appendix C.2.4 for brevity. 4.2.1 Failure Mode of Existing Methods FB solves the zero-shot RL problem in two stages. First, a generalist policy is pre-trained to maximise FB’s Q functions for all tasks sampled from the prior Z (Equation 4.1). Second, the test task is inferred from reward-labelled states (Equation 4.3) and passed to the policy. The first stage relies on an accurate approximation of F(s, a, z) i.e. the long-run dynamics of the environment subject to a policy attempting to solve task z. The second stage relies on an accurate approximation of B(s) i.e. the task associated with reaching state s. If the states in F are replaced by observations that only partially characterise the underlying state, then the BFM will struggle to predict the long-run dynamics, Q functions derived from F will be inaccurate, and the policy will not learn optimal sequences of actions. We call this failure mode state misidentification (Figure 4.2, middle). Likewise, if the states in B are replaced by partial observations, and the reward function depends on the underlying state (§4.1), then the BFM cannot reliably find the task z associated with the set of states that maximise the reward function. We call this failure mode task misidentification (Figure 4.2, left). The failure modes occur together when both models receive partial observations (Figure 4.2, right). 1Equation 4.3 assumes Dlabelled is drawn from the same distribution as D, that is, it assumes both datasets are produced by the same, exploratory behaviour policy. The standard benchmarks for each of these settings only require the agent to solve one task, and so do not allow us to evaluate zero-shot RL capabilities out-of-the-box. As a result, we choose to amend the standard zero-shot RL benchmark, ExORL, such that it tests zero-shot RL with partially observed states and dynamics changes. Partially observed states We amend two of ’s partially observed state environments for the zero-shot RL setting: 1) noisy states, where isotropic zero-mean Gaussian noise with variance σnoise is added to the Markov state, and 2) flickering states, where states are dropped (zeroed) with probability pflick.. We set σnoise = 0.2 and pflick. = 0.2 following a hyperparameter study (Appendix A.1.1). We evaluate on all tasks in the Walker, Cheetah and Quadruped environments. Partially observed changes in dynamics We amend ’s dynamics generalisation tests for the zero-shot RL setting. Environment dynamics are modulated by scaling the mass and damping coefficients in the MuJoCu backend. The agents are trained on datasets collected from environment instances with coefficients scaled to {0.5×, 1.5×} their usual values, then evaluated on environment instances with coefficients scaled by {1.0×, 2.0×}. Scaling by 1.0× tests the agent’s ability to generalise via interpolation within the range seen during training, and scaling by 2.0× tests the agent’s ability to generalise via extrapolation. We use two state-of-the-art zero-shot RL methods as baselines: FB and HILP. We additionally implement a naïve baseline called FB-stack whose input is a stack of the 4 most recent observations and actions, following ’s canonical protocol. Finally, we use FB trained on the underlying MDP as an oracle policy to give us an upper-bound on expected performance. All methods inherit the default hyperparameters from previous works (Jeen et al., 2024; Park et al., 2024b; Touati et al., 2023). We train all methods on datasets collected with an RND behaviour policy as these are the datasets that elicit best performance on ExORL. The RND datasets used in the partially observed states experiments are taken directly from ExORL. For the partially observed change in dynamics experiments, we collect these datasets ourselves by running RND in each of the environments for 5 million learning steps. Our implementation and training protocol exactly match ExORL’s. Memory model We use a GRU as our memory model. GRUs are the most performant memory model on POPGym which tests partially observed single-task RL methods. We find these results hold for partially observed zero-shot RL too, as discussed in §4.4.1. We set the context length L = 32; see Appendix C.1.8 for a hyperparameter study and further discussion. Evaluation protocol We evaluate the cumulative reward achieved by all methods across 5 seeds, with task scores reported as per the best practice recommendations of. Concretely, we run each algorithm for 1 million learning steps, evaluating task scores at checkpoints of 20, 000 steps. At each checkpoint, we perform 10 rollouts, record the score of each, and find the interquartile mean (IQM). We average across seeds at each checkpoint. We extract task scores from the learning step for which the all-task IQM is maximised across seeds. Results are reported with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals in plots and standard deviations in tables. Aggregation across tasks, domains and datasets is always performed by evaluating the IQM. 4.3.2 Partially Observed States Figure 4.3 compares the zero-shot performance of all algorithms on our noisy and flickering variants of the standard ExORL environments.
